        required: false
        default: ''
    upstream-url:
        description: The upstream cache to filter against before pushing.
        required: false
        default: https://cache.nixos.org
    default-branch-ref:
        description: >-
            The ref permitted to renew the lease. The cache enforces this itself; this input only avoids a
            request that would be refused.
        required: false
        default: refs/heads/main
    trusted-public-key:
        description: >-
            The public half of the signing key, in Nix's `name:base64` form, so this job can verify what it
            substitutes from the cache.
        required: false
        # A metadata default, like `cache-url` above: the public key is deployment identity, not a
        # secret, and ADR 0013 makes action metadata the one place deployment identity may appear.
        # Without a default here every consuming repository would have to learn and paste the key,
        # and one that forgot would fail signature verification on every substitution — which Nix
        # reports as a cache miss, so the job would silently compile from source while the cache
        # looked healthy. The login script bakes in the same value (`public_key_default` in
        # scripts/cache-login.sh), so a laptop and a runner learn the key the same way.
        default: pkg-cache.loopholelabs.io-1:JC2XK3HyAUXteubthi/pUEM0iokE6YyOGFURMB4hsRE=
    push:
        description: Set to false to use the cache read-only.
        required: false
        default: 'true'
    determinate-nix-action-version:
        description: Which release of the Determinate Nix installer action to use.
        required: false
        default: v3

runs:
    using: composite
    steps:
        # Provision the cache read credential BEFORE Determinate is installed and its daemon starts.
        # Determinate synthesizes the netrc the daemon reads (/nix/var/determinate/netrc) at daemon start,
        # merging every file listed under authentication.additionalNetrcSources — and that start-up
        # synthesis is the only reliable one on these runners. A later re-synthesis is gated on the FlakeHub
        # login, whose transient failures otherwise leave cache reads at 401 and every build recompiling
        # from source. Writing the credential and the config here, before the daemon exists, means its
        # start-up synthesis merges the credential and the FlakeHub failure never gets to gate it
        # (docs.determinate.systems, migrate-to-flakehub-cache).
        - name: Provision the cachet read credential before Determinate starts
          shell: bash
          env:
              CACHET_CACHE_URL: ${{ inputs.cache-url }}
              CACHET_AUDIENCE: ${{ inputs.audience }}
          run: |
              set -euo pipefail

              # The OIDC token authenticates this job; nothing is stored and the runner is authorised
              # because it is provably ours (docs/contracts.md). This is minted here, without Nix, because
              # Determinate is not installed yet.
              if [ -z "${ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL:-}" ]; then
                echo "cachet: this job cannot mint an OIDC token." >&2
                echo "  Add 'permissions: { contents: read, id-token: write }' to the job." >&2
                exit 1
              fi
              token="$(curl -fsSL \
                -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN}" \
                "${ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL}&audience=${CACHET_AUDIENCE}" | jq -r '.value')"
              host="$(printf '%s' "${CACHET_CACHE_URL}" | sed -e 's#^https\?://##' -e 's#/.*$##')"

              # The credential file: real, outside the Nix store, 0600, root-owned, as Determinate requires.
              sudo mkdir -p /etc/nix /etc/determinate
              printf 'machine %s login cachet password %s\n' "${host}" "${token}" \
                | sudo tee /etc/nix/netrc >/dev/null
              sudo chmod 600 /etc/nix/netrc

              # Register it under authentication.additionalNetrcSources. Determinate is not installed yet,
              # so the config usually does not exist; merge with jq when it does so anything the installer
              # pre-seeds survives.
              if [ -f /etc/determinate/config.json ]; then
                sudo cat /etc/determinate/config.json \
                  | jq '.authentication.additionalNetrcSources = ((.authentication.additionalNetrcSources // []) + ["/etc/nix/netrc"] | unique)' \
                  | sudo tee /etc/determinate/config.json.tmp >/dev/null
                sudo mv /etc/determinate/config.json.tmp /etc/determinate/config.json
              else
                printf '{"authentication":{"additionalNetrcSources":["/etc/nix/netrc"]}}\n' \
                  | sudo tee /etc/determinate/config.json >/dev/null
              fi
              echo "cachet: read credential provisioned before Determinate starts"

        # Determinate Nix is the one distribution everywhere, including on laptops (ADR 0008).
        - uses: DeterminateSystems/determinate-nix-action@v3.21.9
          with:
              # Add the cache and its trusted key at install time, so the daemon starts already knowing
              # them. Adding them afterwards in the Configure step proved ineffective — the daemon never
              # queried cachet at all — because a substituter and its trusted key reach the daemon only when
              # it reads its config at start. extra-substituters and extra-trusted-public-keys accumulate
              # (they use the extra- prefix), so this adds cachet alongside cache.nixos.org rather than
              # replacing it.
              extra-conf: |
                  extra-substituters = ${{ inputs.cache-url }}
                  extra-trusted-public-keys = ${{ inputs.trusted-public-key }}

        # Log out of FlakeHub, which the determinate-nix-action step above logged into on its own. On a
        # runner granting id-token: write — which this action requires to mint its own cachet OIDC token —
        # Determinate mints a second OIDC token for FlakeHub and logs in, and that login adds
        # https://cache.flakehub.com to the daemon's active substituters. This deployment is not a FlakeHub
        # Cache customer, so every narinfo lookup then answers 401 ("User is not authorized for this
        # resource") before it falls through to cachet: an error-level log line and a wasted round trip on
        # every request, on a build that still succeeds. Logging out returns the substituter set to the
        # logged-out state, in which cache.flakehub.com is absent — verified against a local Determinate
        # install, where `determinate-nixd status` reports logged-out and `nix config show substituters`
        # omits FlakeHub. cachet's own read credential is the netrc merged from additionalNetrcSources and
        # is independent of the FlakeHub login, so the Configure step's auth probe below still reports 404.
        - name: Log out of FlakeHub Cache, which this deployment does not use
          shell: bash
          run: |
              set -euo pipefail
              # `|| true`: a job without id-token never logged in, so logout is a no-op there rather than a
              # failure, and this action must not fail a build over a cache it does not even use.
              sudo determinate-nixd auth logout || true
              echo "cachet: FlakeHub login status after logout:"
              sudo determinate-nixd status || true

        - name: Configure cachet
          shell: bash
          env:
              CACHET_CACHE_URL: ${{ inputs.cache-url }}
              CACHET_AUDIENCE: ${{ inputs.audience }}
              CACHET_TRUSTED_PUBLIC_KEY: ${{ inputs.trusted-public-key }}
              CACHET_SIGNING_KEY: ${{ inputs.signing-key }}
              CACHET_PROJECT: ${{ inputs.project }}
              CACHET_ROOTS: ${{ inputs.roots }}
              CACHET_UPSTREAM_URL: ${{ inputs.upstream-url }}
              CACHET_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF: ${{ inputs.default-branch-ref }}
              CACHET_PUSH: ${{ inputs.push }}
          run: |
              set -euo pipefail

              # The read credential and its Determinate config were provisioned before the daemon started
              # (the first step of this action), so the daemon's start-up synthesis already merged the
              # credential into the netrc it reads. There is nothing to do here for the netrc.

              # The substituter and trusted key are added at install time now (the extra-conf on the
              # determinate-nix-action step above), so the daemon starts already knowing them. They are not
              # written here: a substituter added after the daemon has started is never consulted, which is
              # why the last run authenticated yet never queried cachet.

              # Confirm the daemon's netrc authenticates against cachet, so a regression surfaces in the log
              # rather than as a silent rebuild: a 404 means the credential is present and authenticated —
              # the probed path is simply absent — while a 401 means it is not.
              daemon_netrc="$(nix config show netrc-file 2>/dev/null || echo /nix/var/determinate/netrc)"
              probe_code="$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --netrc-file "${daemon_netrc}" \
                "${CACHET_CACHE_URL%/}/0000000000000000000000000000000a.narinfo" 2>/dev/null || echo 000)"
              echo "cachet: read auth probe returned ${probe_code} (404 = authenticated, 401 = not)"

              # The signing key is written where only this runner can read it, and never leaves it (ADR 0004).
              key_file="${RUNNER_TEMP}/cachet-signing.key"
              printf '%s' "${CACHET_SIGNING_KEY}" > "${key_file}"
              chmod 600 "${key_file}"
              echo "CACHET_SIGNING_KEY_FILE=${key_file}" >> "${GITHUB_ENV}"

              # Everything the post step reads is exported to the job environment here, and this is the
              # only place any of it is resolved. A step-level `env:` block is scoped to the step it sits
              # on, so passing these to the nested action as `with:` inputs left the post step reading
              # empty strings and declining to push, silently, on every run.
              #
              # The project name defaults to owner-and-name rather than the bare repository name.
              #
              # why: this cache serves more than one organisation, so two repositories can share a name.
              # A lease is filed under the project name and a renewal replaces the previous document
              # wholesale, so two same-named repositories defaulting to one project would overwrite each
              # other's lease — and each would then stop protecting the other's closure, making live
              # paths collectable (Invariant GC-NEVER-EATS-THE-LIVING). Including the owner makes the
              # default unique by construction rather than by everyone remembering to pass `project`.
              project="${CACHET_PROJECT}"
              if [ -z "${project}" ]; then
                project="${GITHUB_REPOSITORY//\//-}"
              fi
              # why: the heredoc form rather than `NAME=value`. `roots` takes several installables and the
              # post step splits it on any whitespace, so a caller writing them one per line with a YAML
              # block scalar is using the documented shape — and a bare `NAME=value` line cannot express
              # a newline. GitHub rejects the whole file with "Invalid format" when it sees the
              # continuation, which fails the step for a reason that points nowhere near the cause.
              #
              # The delimiter is fixed and long enough not to occur in a flake installable, and the
              # values here are action inputs rather than anything a request supplies.
              env_file() {
                printf '%s<<CACHET_EOF_1c7f\n%s\nCACHET_EOF_1c7f\n' "$1" "$2" >> "${GITHUB_ENV}"
              }
              env_file CACHET_CACHE_URL "${CACHET_CACHE_URL}"
              env_file CACHET_AUDIENCE "${CACHET_AUDIENCE}"
              env_file CACHET_PROJECT "${project}"
              env_file CACHET_ROOTS "${CACHET_ROOTS}"
              env_file CACHET_UPSTREAM_URL "${CACHET_UPSTREAM_URL}"
              env_file CACHET_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF "${CACHET_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF}"
              env_file CACHET_PUSH "${CACHET_PUSH}"

              echo "cachet: configured ${CACHET_CACHE_URL} as a substituter for project ${project}"

        # The nested JavaScript action: its main step snapshots the store, and its post step, on success
        # only, does the push. It takes no inputs, because the step above resolved all of them into the
        # job environment.
        # why: the full owner/repo/path@ref form rather than `./post`. A composite action resolves a
        # relative `./post` against the consumer's GITHUB_WORKSPACE rather than this action's own
        # directory, so a cross-repo consumer looked for `<workspace>/post` and failed with "Can't find
        # 'action.yml' under .../post". Naming the repository resolves the nested action independently of
        # where the consumer checked out. It is pinned to the v1 major tag, which every release in the 1.x
        # line moves forward, so the composite and its post action always come from the same line.
        - uses: agx-runtime/cachet-action/post@v1
action.yml
dist

[package]
name = "cachet-push"
description = "The push pipeline as a native library: store snapshot and diff, upstream filtering, zstd staging, NAR-before-narinfo upload, and lease renewal. Consumed by the CLI and the GitHub Action."
edition.workspace = true
version.workspace = true
publish.workspace = true
license.workspace = true

workspace = true

[dependencies]
cachet-core = { path = "../cachet-core" }
cachet-crypto = { path = "../cachet-crypto" }
cachet-api = { path = "../cachet-api" }
serde.workspace = true
serde_json.workspace = true
# why: the pipeline fans out presence probes sixteen wide and streams
# bodies off disk; nothing else in the tree gives a native runtime with
# completion-based file I/O, and hand-rolling one is not on the table.
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["fs", "io-util", "macros", "process", "rt-multi-thread", "time"] }
# why: the wire half of the pipeline. rustls keeps OpenSSL's platform
# lottery off laptops and runners alike, and the stream feature is what
# the multipart plan's ranged reads ride.
reqwest = { version = "0.12", default-features = false, features = ["json", "rustls-tls", "stream"] }
# why: the probe pools bound concurrency with buffer_unordered; the
# alternative is a handwritten worker pool around JoinSet for no gain.
futures-util = "0.3"

[dev-dependencies]
# why: adapter tests stage into temporary directories; hand-rolled
# uniqueness is an entropy bug waiting to happen.
tempfile = "3"

[dev-dependencies]

# why: push rides the same runtime cachet-push already pins; the CLI adds

# why: keygen needs 32 bytes of OS entropy on the native side only; the
# worker's js feature ships separately.

input.content:
# The action consumers wire into their CI: install Determinate Nix trusting
# this cache, provision the job's read credential before the daemon starts,
# download the pinned cachet binary, and hand the push phases to the nested
# main/post action. Signing happens server-side, so the action holds no key
# material; the job's OIDC token is the only credential it ever touches.
name: cachet setup
description: >-
  Install Determinate Nix wired to a cachet deployment, then push what the
  job builds. Needs `permissions: { contents: read, id-token: write }`.
author: nox-systems

inputs:
  cache-url:
    description: The cache's base URL.
    required: true
  roots:
    description: >-
      Flake installables whose closures this project keeps. Their outputs
      are pushed unconditionally and, on the default branch, become the
      project's garbage-collection lease.
    required: false
    default: ""
  audience:
    description: The OIDC audience the cache requires.
    required: false
    default: cachet
  project:
    description: >-
      The lease name for this repository. Defaults to the owner and name
      joined by a hyphen (`my-org-my-repo`), because a renewal replaces the
      lease wholesale: two same-named repositories in one org would
      otherwise overwrite each other's.
    required: false
    default: ""
  upstream-url:
    description: The upstream cache to filter against before pushing.
    required: false
    default: https://cache.nixos.org
  default-branch-ref:
    description: >-
      The ref permitted to renew the lease. The cache enforces this itself;
      this input only avoids a request that would be refused.
    required: false
    default: refs/heads/main
  push:
    description: Set to false to use the cache read-only.
    required: false
    default: "true"
  cachet-version:
    description: The cachet release to download and run.
    required: false
    default: 0.0.1

runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    # Provision the read credential BEFORE Determinate is installed and its
    # daemon starts. determinate-nixd synthesizes the netrc the daemon reads
    # at daemon start, merging every file under
    # authentication.additionalNetrcSources, and that startup synthesis is
    # the only reliable one on these runners. Writing the credential and its
    # registration here means the daemon's start-up synthesis sees both.
    - name: Provision the cachet read credential before Determinate starts
      shell: bash
      env:
        CACHET_CACHE_URL: ${{ inputs.cache-url }}
        CACHET_AUDIENCE: ${{ inputs.audience }}
      run: |
        set -euo pipefail

        # The OIDC token authenticates this job's reads; the runner is
        # authorized because it is provably the org's CI. Minted here,
        # without nix, because Determinate is not installed yet. This check
        # fails the job on purpose: every later step assumes the token.
        if [ -z "${ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL:-}" ]; then
          echo "cachet: this job cannot mint an OIDC token." >&2
          echo "  Add 'permissions: { contents: read, id-token: write }' to the job." >&2
          exit 1
        fi
        token="$(curl -fsSL \
          -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN}" \
          "${ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL}&audience=${CACHET_AUDIENCE}" | jq -r '.value')"
        host="$(printf '%s' "${CACHET_CACHE_URL}" | sed -e 's#^https\?://##' -e 's#/.*$##')"

        # The credential file: real, outside the nix store, 0600.
        sudo mkdir -p /etc/nix /etc/determinate
        printf 'machine %s login cachet password %s\n' "${host}" "${token}" \
          | sudo tee /etc/nix/netrc >/dev/null
        sudo chmod 600 /etc/nix/netrc

        # Register it under authentication.additionalNetrcSources, merging
        # when the installer pre-seeded the file.
        if [ -f /etc/determinate/config.json ]; then
          sudo cat /etc/determinate/config.json \
            | jq '.authentication.additionalNetrcSources = ((.authentication.additionalNetrcSources // []) + ["/etc/nix/netrc"] | unique)' \
            | sudo tee /etc/determinate/config.json.tmp >/dev/null
          sudo mv /etc/determinate/config.json.tmp /etc/determinate/config.json
        else
          printf '{"authentication":{"additionalNetrcSources":["/etc/nix/netrc"]}}\n' \
            | sudo tee /etc/determinate/config.json >/dev/null
        fi

        # The deployment names its own signing key: fetch the public half
        # from the worker rather than asking consumers to paste it. This
        # doubles as the connectivity check: a cache that cannot answer its
        # public config fails the job here, before the build starts.
        public_key="$(curl -fsSL "${CACHET_CACHE_URL%/}/api/public/config" | jq -r '.publicKey')"
        echo "CACHET_TRUSTED_PUBLIC_KEY=${public_key}" >> "${GITHUB_ENV}"
        echo "cachet: read credential provisioned before Determinate starts"

    - uses: DeterminateSystems/determinate-nix-action@61cbfe2efc2d4e7a8a6d56967c3c1058e846c858 # v3.21.9
      with:
        # The substituter and trusted key ride the install because a
        # substituter added after the daemon has started is never consulted.
        extra-conf: |
          extra-substituters = ${{ inputs.cache-url }}
          extra-trusted-public-keys = ${{ env.CACHET_TRUSTED_PUBLIC_KEY }}

    # The Determinate installer logged into FlakeHub on this runner (any job
    # granting id-token: write gets one), which adds cache.flakehub.com as a
    # substituter: every lookup then pays a 401 round trip before falling
    # through to cachet. Log out; the cachet credential is independent.
    - name: Log out of FlakeHub Cache, which this deployment does not use
      shell: bash
      run: |
        set -euo pipefail
        # `|| true`: a job without id-token never logged in, so logout is a
        # no-op there, and this action must not fail a build over a cache it
        # does not use.
        sudo determinate-nixd auth logout || true
        sudo determinate-nixd status || true

    - name: Download and verify the cachet binary
      shell: bash
      env:
        CACHET_VERSION: ${{ inputs.cachet-version }}
      run: |
        set -euo pipefail
        case "${{ runner.os }}-${{ runner.arch }}" in
          Linux-X64) triple="x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu" ;;
          Linux-ARM64) triple="aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu" ;;
          macOS-X64) triple="x86_64-apple-darwin" ;;
          macOS-ARM64) triple="aarch64-apple-darwin" ;;
          *)
            echo "cachet: no cachet release for ${{ runner.os }}-${{ runner.arch }}" >&2
            exit 1
            ;;
        esac
        base="https://github.com/nox-systems/cachet/releases/download/v${CACHET_VERSION}"
        artifact="cachet-${triple}.tar.xz"
        work="$(mktemp -d)"
        # The checksum verifies before the archive opens: a tampered or
        # truncated download fails the job, it does not limp onward.
        curl -fsSL -o "${work}/${artifact}" "${base}/${artifact}"
        curl -fsSL -o "${work}/${artifact}.sha256" "${base}/${artifact}.sha256"
        (cd "${work}" && shasum -a 256 -c "${artifact}.sha256")
        install_dir="${RUNNER_TEMP}/cachet-bin"
        mkdir -p "${install_dir}"
        tar -xJf "${work}/${artifact}" -C "${install_dir}" --strip-components=1
        rm -rf "${work}"
        echo "CACHET_BIN=${install_dir}/cachet" >> "${GITHUB_ENV}"
        "${install_dir}/cachet" --version

    - name: Configure cachet
      shell: bash
      env:
        CACHET_CACHE_URL: ${{ inputs.cache-url }}
        CACHET_AUDIENCE: ${{ inputs.audience }}
        CACHET_PROJECT: ${{ inputs.project }}
        CACHET_ROOTS: ${{ inputs.roots }}
        CACHET_UPSTREAM_URL: ${{ inputs.upstream-url }}
        CACHET_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF: ${{ inputs.default-branch-ref }}
        CACHET_PUSH: ${{ inputs.push }}
      run: |
        set -euo pipefail

        # Confirm the daemon's netrc authenticates against cachet, so a
        # regression surfaces in the log rather than as a silent rebuild: a
        # 404 means the credential is present and authenticated (the probed
        # path is simply absent), while a 401 means it is not.
        daemon_netrc="$(nix config show netrc-file 2>/dev/null || echo /nix/var/determinate/netrc)"
        probe_code="$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' --netrc-file "${daemon_netrc}" \
          "${CACHET_CACHE_URL%/}/0000000000000000000000000000000a.narinfo" 2>/dev/null || echo 000)"
        echo "cachet: read auth probe returned ${probe_code} (404 = authenticated, 401 = not)"

        # Everything the post step reads is exported here, and this is the
        # only place any of it is resolved. A step-level `env:` block is
        # scoped to its own step, so passing these to the nested action as
        # `with:` inputs left the post step reading empty strings.
        project="${CACHET_PROJECT}"
        if [ -z "${project}" ]; then
          project="${GITHUB_REPOSITORY//\//-}"
        fi
        # why: the heredoc form rather than `NAME=value`. `roots` takes
        # several installables and the post step splits on any whitespace,
        # so a caller writing them one per line with a YAML block scalar is
        # using the documented shape, and a bare `NAME=value` line cannot
        # express a newline: GitHub rejects the whole file with "Invalid
        # format" when it sees the continuation.
        env_file() {
          printf '%s<<CACHET_EOF_1c7f\n%s\nCACHET_EOF_1c7f\n' "$1" "$2" >> "${GITHUB_ENV}"
        }
        env_file CACHET_CACHE_URL "${CACHET_CACHE_URL%/}"
        env_file CACHET_AUDIENCE "${CACHET_AUDIENCE}"
        env_file CACHET_PROJECT "${project}"
        env_file CACHET_ROOTS "${CACHET_ROOTS}"
        env_file CACHET_UPSTREAM_URL "${CACHET_UPSTREAM_URL}"
        env_file CACHET_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF "${CACHET_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF}"
        env_file CACHET_PUSH "${CACHET_PUSH}"
        echo "cachet: configured ${CACHET_CACHE_URL} as a substituter for project ${project}"

    # The nested JavaScript action: its main step snapshots the store, and
    # its post step, on success only, pushes. It reads no inputs, because
    # the step above resolved everything into the job environment.
    # why: the full owner/repo/path@ref form rather than `./post`. A
    # composite action resolves a relative `./post` against the consumer's
    # workspace rather than this action's own directory, so a cross-repo
    # consumer failed with "Can't find 'action.yml'". The ref names the v1
    # major tag, which every release in the 1.x line moves forward, so the
    # composite and its post action always come from the same line.
    - uses: nox-systems/cachet/action/post@v1

name: cachet push
description: >-
  Snapshots the nix store at main time and pushes what the job added at post
  time, on success only. The cachet setup composite action wraps this; it is
  not meant to be used directly.

# why: no inputs. The composite resolves every value and exports it to the
# job environment, which is what both phases read. Declaring inputs here as
# well would hand the post step a second, differently-named source of the
# same configuration (GitHub exposes an input as INPUT_<NAME>, not as the
# name the code reads), and that mismatch is the bug that once made this
# step decline to push while reporting success.
runs:
  using: node24
  main: main.cjs
  post: post.cjs
  # why: on success only. A failed build must never populate the cache or
  # refresh a lease: that is what keeps a broken artifact from becoming the
  # one everybody substitutes.
  post-if: success()

content.text:
Yes — admins are deployment configuration, not database rows. `CACHET_ADMINS` is a comma-separated var of GitHub logins, set alongside `CACHET_ORGS` at deploy time (alchemy in `infra/` for real deploys, `[vars]` in `wrangler.toml` for the lane). The request path works like this: the caller authenticates with their GitHub token or browser session, the worker resolves their *login* through the verdict path (GitHub `/user` plus org-membership check, cached in KV), and `require_admin` compares that login against the env list before serving `/api/self/*` routes (GC reports, stats).

Two deliberate consequences: there is no admin-granting API (you can't escalate through the worker by calling it), and adding or removing an admin means editing config and redeploying — which for this system is also the audit trail, since the var lives in infra code. A membership set that changes rarely and is owned by the same person who owns the deployment doesn't want a database; it wants `terraform apply`-style friction.

The one rule to keep straight: it's *logins*, not emails — the verdict resolves a GitHub username, and that's what the list must contain.

content.text: The gate works — it caught shellcheck style findings in cargo-dist's *generated* `release.yml`. Those bytes belong to the generator, so the fix is: syntax-and-expression checking for the generated workflow, full shellcheck discipline for the files we author:

input.new_string:
# Every workflow and action file the repo ships, with shellcheck on
        # the PATH so the `run:` blocks lint too. actionlint only detects
        # action files by their project-relative name, so the sources land
        # under a scratch project layout and the scan runs argument-free.
        # release.yml is cargo-dist's own output (regenerate, never edit):
        # it gets actionlint's syntax and expression checks in a second
        # project, but shellcheck's style findings belong to the generator,
        # so its `run:` blocks are not linted here.
        actionlint =
          pkgs.runCommand "actionlint"
            {
              nativeBuildInputs = [
                pkgs.actionlint
                pkgs.shellcheck
                pkgs.nodejs_22
              ];
            }
            ''
              mkdir -p proj/.git
              cp -r ${../.github} proj/.github
              rm -f proj/.github/workflows/release.yml
              cp -r ${../action} proj/action
              (cd proj && actionlint)
              mkdir -p proj-gen/.git proj-gen/.github/workflows
              cp ${../.github/workflows/release.yml} proj-gen/.github/workflows/release.yml
              (cd proj-gen && actionlint -shellcheck "" release.yml)
              node --check ${../action/post/main.cjs}
              node --check ${../action/post/post.cjs}
              touch $out
            '';

input.new_string:
# aws-lc and the C zstd crate do not build for wasm32-unknown-unknown;
# ruzstd supplies the worker's only decompression need. ring carries the
# same incompatibility, but the two native crates (cachet-push, cachet-cli)
# need TLS on hosts and rustls's only remaining provider choices are ring
# or aws-lc, so ring is allowed through exactly the rustls chain and no
# further: a new dependant outside these wrappers fails the gate, and the
# worker's artifact is scanned for it regardless (§5, check-wasm-hygiene).

    { name = "ring", reason = "does not build for wasm32-unknown-unknown; allowed only as the rustls chain's native TLS provider", wrappers = ["rustls", "rustls-webpki"] },

---
# The workerd lane's deployment shape (docs/testing/workerd.md): the same
# module directory and module rules the real deployment uses, against
# workerd's local R2 emulation. The compatibility date trails the newest
# workerd in the devshell, and raising it is a deliberate lane decision.
name = "cachet-worker-lane"
compatibility_date = "2026-05-01"
main = "../crates/cachet-worker/build/index.js"
rules = [
  { type = "CompiledWasm", globs = ["**/*.wasm"], fallthrough = true },
]

[[r2_buckets]]
binding = "CACHE_BUCKET"
bucket_name = "cachet-lane"

# Verdicts, sessions, and OAuth state live in KV; the lane namespace is
# local-emulated, so the id is a label rather than an account resource.
[[kv_namespaces]]
binding = "CACHET_KV"
id = "cachet-lane"

# The lane deployment's auth configuration: a fixed org, audience, and
# branch; CACHET_JWKS_URL and CACHET_GITHUB_API_URL join per run via
# `wrangler dev --var`, pointing at the driver's stub services (the URLs
# are transport configuration; the keys authenticate the tokens, not the
# address they came from).
[vars]
CACHET_ORGS = "lane-org"
CACHET_AUDIENCE = "cachet-lane"
CACHET_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF = "refs/heads/main"
CACHET_HOST = "cachet.lane.invalid"
CACHET_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID = "lane-oauth-client"
# The laptop token's user is the lane's admin; a second member token
# exercises forbidden_admin.
CACHET_ADMINS = "lane-dev"
# The OAuth web endpoints join per run via --var, like the API URL. The UI
# origin is fixed here so the callback's redirect branch is lane-tested;
# absent in a deployment without a UI, where the callback answers 204.
CACHET_UI_ORIGIN = "https://ui.lane.invalid"
# The collector runs armed with grace zeroed: the lane's seeded objects
# are seconds old and must still be sweepable.
CACHET_GC_GRACE_MS = "0"

# The deployment's collector binding; the lane invokes the scheduled
# handler directly over its dev endpoint.
[triggers]
crons = ["0 5 * * *"]

* Mutually exclusive with {@link script}, {@link vite}, and
   * {@link main} — a source is self-contained; a provider that needs a
   * custom entry takes it in its own `options`.
   */
  source?: WorkerSourceDescriptor;
  logpush?: boolean;
  /**
   * Cloudflare Workers Observability settings. Controls Workers Logs
   * (`logs`) and Workers Traces (`traces`), each with their own
   * `enabled`, `headSamplingRate`, and `persist` toggles.
   *
   * If omitted, defaults to `{ enabled: true, logs: { enabled: true,
   * invocationLogs: true } }`. Traces are off by default — opt in via
   * `traces: { enabled: true, ... }`.
   */
  observability?: WorkerObservability;
  /**
   * Workers Cache settings. When `enabled` is `true`, Cloudflare checks a
   * regionally tiered cache in front of the Worker on every HTTP request —
   * cache hits are served from the edge without invoking the Worker at all.
   * The Worker controls what gets cached via standard response headers
   * (`Cache-Control`, `Cache-Tag`, `Vary`), including
   * `stale-while-revalidate`.
   *
   * Set `crossVersionCache: true` to share cached responses across Worker
   * versions (by default the cache is scoped to a single version, so every
   * deploy starts cold).
   *
   * If omitted, Workers Cache is disabled — unless the Worker's init phase
   * enables it via `yield* Cloudflare.cache()`, which is the preferred way
   * for Effect-native Workers (and also returns the runtime purge client).
   * When both are set, this prop takes precedence.
   *
   * @see https://blog.cloudflare.com/workers-cache/
   */
  cache?: WorkerCache;
  tags?: string[];
  /**
   * Path to the Worker's entry module. Bundled with rolldown before
   * upload. Mutually exclusive with {@link script} — provide at most one.
   * Omit both (with {@link assets} set) to deploy an assets-only Worker.
   *
   * A `.py` entry deploys a Python Worker instead: no bundling runs — the
   * entry plus every sibling `.py` file upload as Python modules, the
   * `python_workers` compatibility flag is added, and dependencies from
   * `pyproject.toml` (or a prebuilt `python_modules/` directory) are
   * vendored alongside. See the Python Workers section above.
   */
  main?: string;
  /**
   * Raw module source for the Worker. When provided, bundling is bypassed
   * entirely and this string is uploaded as a single ESM module
   * (`main.js`). Useful for tiny inline workers (tests, fixtures,
   * one-offs) and any case where you've already produced the final
   * bundle elsewhere. Mutually exclusive with {@link main}.
   */
  script?: string;
  compatibility?: {
    date?: string;
    flags?: ("nodejs_compat" | "nodejs_als" | (string & {}))[];
  };
  limits?: WorkerLimits;
  placement?: WorkerPlacement;
  /**
   * Tracks Durable Object and Workflow exports for Effect-native Workers only.
   * Populated automatically from bindings; do not set manually.
   * @internal
   */
  exports?: Record<string, DurableObjectExport | WorkflowExport>;
  /**
   * Environment variables and native Cloudflare Bindings to bind to
   * the Worker. Accepts:
   *
   * - Resource references (R2 bucket, KV namespace, D1 database,
   *   another Worker, Durable Object, etc.) — emitted as the
   *   corresponding native binding.
   * - `effect/Config` values (`Config.redacted`, `Config.string`,
   *   `Config.number`, …) — resolved at deploy time and bound as
   *   `secret_text` on Cloudflare regardless of the `Config`
   *   constructor used. See
   *   [Secrets & env](/cloudflare/security/secrets-env).
   * - Literal values — routed by shape: `Redacted<string>` →
   *   `secret_text`, `string` → `plain_text`, anything else → `json`.
   * - `Output` values that resolve to a plain env value (e.g.
   *   `Alchemy.makeRandom`) — classified at deploy time by their
   *   resolved value using the literal rules above. Whole-resource
   *   Outputs (`Output.of(bucket)`) are rejected at deploy time; bind
   *   the resource itself instead.
   *
   * In Effect-native Workers you can alternatively `yield*` a
   * `Config` in the Init phase to register the binding implicitly;
   * `env` is the only option for async (non-Effect) Workers.
   */
  env?: Bindings;
  /**
   * Cron expressions that trigger the Worker's scheduled handler.
   *
   * This is how async (non-Effect) Workers configure Cron Triggers — the
   * entry module exports its own `scheduled` handler and this prop attaches
   * the schedules at deploy time. Effect-native Workers usually skip this
   * prop and call `Cloudflare.Workers.cron(expression, handler)` in the Init
   * phase instead, which attaches the expression and registers the runtime
   * listener in one step.
   *
   * Pass an empty array to remove all Cron Triggers.
   */
  crons?: string[];
  /**
   * Tail Workers that consume this Worker's execution traces. Each entry is
   * another {@link Worker} (or a literal script name) that exports a `tail()`
   * handler; after each invocation of this Worker, Cloudflare delivers the
   * invocation's trace events (console logs, exceptions, event metadata) to
   * every listed consumer.
   *
   * Pass the consumer Worker resource directly — Alchemy resolves it to its
   * deployed script name and deploys the consumer before this Worker — or a
   * plain script name string for a tail Worker managed outside this stack.
   *
   * Changing the list is an in-place update. Omitting the prop (or passing
   * `[]`) deploys this Worker with no tail consumers attached.
   *
   * @see https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/observability/logs/tail-workers/
   */
  tailConsumers?: (string | Worker)[];
  /**
   * Streaming Tail Workers that consume this Worker's execution events as
   * they happen. Each entry is another {@link Worker} (or a literal script
   * name) that exports a `tailStream()` handler; Cloudflare invokes it with
   * the invocation's `onset` event *while this Worker is still executing*,
   * and the returned handler receives every subsequent event of the session
   * (`log`, `spanOpen`, ...) ending with the terminal `outcome`.
   *
   * This differs from {@link tailConsumers}: a plain tail consumer's `tail()`
   * handler receives the completed `TraceItem`s only after the producer's
   * invocation finishes, while a streaming tail consumer observes events
   * live, per-session, during execution.
   *
   * Pass the consumer Worker resource directly — Alchemy resolves it to its
   * deployed script name and deploys the consumer before this Worker — or a
   * plain script name string for a streaming tail Worker managed outside
   * this stack.
   *
   * Changing the list is an in-place update. Omitting the prop (or passing
   * `[]`) deploys this Worker with no streaming tail consumers attached.
   *
   * Streaming tail workers are experimental on Cloudflare's cloud: the
   * configuration deploys, but production does not yet deliver events —
   * Cloudflare rejects the `streaming_tail_worker` compatibility flag as
   * "experimental and cannot yet be used in Workers deployed to
   * Cloudflare", so a deployed consumer cannot enable its `tailStream()`
   * handler. Under `alchemy dev`, local delivery is fully emulated.
   *
   * @see https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/observability/logs/tail-workers/
   */
  streamingTailConsumers?: (string | Worker)[];
  /**
   * The Worker's custom domain: one canonical hostname, plus optional
   * `aliases` that also serve the Worker and `redirects` that 301 to the
   * canonical name. A bare string is shorthand for `{ name }`. Pin the
   * zone with `zoneId` / `zone` / `zoneName` (same as {@link routes});
   * otherwise each hostname is looked up by name. The zone must already
   * exist in the account.
   *
   * When set, `https://<name>` becomes the Worker's primary `url` output,
   * ranking above the `workers.dev` URL. See {@link WorkerDomainConfig}.
   *
   * Omitting the prop leaves custom domains unmanaged — attachments made
   * outside Alchemy are preserved. Pass `null` to explicitly detach every
   * custom domain (and remove their redirect rules).
   */
  domain?: string | WorkerDomainConfig | null;
  /**
   * Zone routes that map URL patterns to this Worker. Equivalent to Wrangler's
   * `routes` array — provide `zoneName` or `zoneId` (or `zone`) alongside each
   * `pattern`. When the zone is omitted, it is inferred from the pattern's
   * hostname.
   */
  routes?: WorkerRouteConfig[];
  /**
   * Extra bundler options applied on top of the standard rolldown
   * input/output options used to build this Worker. Includes the generic
   * bundle extras (pure-annotation packages, bundle analyzer) plus an
   * `output` field of rolldown output overrides (e.g. `codeSplitting`
   * groups) merged over Alchemy's defaults. See {@link WorkerBuildOptions}.
   */
  build?: WorkerBuildOptions;
  /**
   * Whether to bundle {@link main} with rolldown before upload.
   *
   * Set to `false` when `main` already points at a complete,
   * runtime-ready ESM Worker produced by an external tool (OpenNext,
   * a separate rolldown/esbuild pipeline, etc.). The entry and every
   * file around it matching {@link rules} are uploaded byte-for-byte —
   * no bundling, no minification, no transformation. Module names are
   * the files' POSIX paths relative to the entry's directory, matching
   * Wrangler's `no_bundle` contract.
   *
   * Re-bundling such artifacts is unsafe: dynamic `import()` calls the
   * upstream tool relies on can be rewritten in ways that break runtime
   * behavior.
   *
   * Durable Object and Workflow classes must be exported by the prebuilt
   * entry itself — {@link exports} is not applied when `bundle` is
   * `false`.
   *
   * @default true
   */
  bundle?: boolean;
  /**
   * Module rules selecting which files in the directory containing
   * {@link main} are uploaded as additional modules when {@link bundle}
   * is `false`. Each rule's globs are matched against POSIX-style paths
   * relative to that directory, mirroring Wrangler's `rules`
   * configuration. When provided, these rules replace
   * {@link defaultModuleRules}.
   *
   * @default defaultModuleRules — ESModule (`**\/*.js`, `**\/*.mjs`), CompiledWasm (`**\/*.wasm`), Text (`**\/*.txt`, `**\/*.html`, `**\/*.sql`), Data (`**\/*.bin`)
   */
  rules?: ModuleRule[];
  /**
   * Options for the local dev server that runs this Worker under `alchemy dev`.
   * Each Worker is served on its own port.
   *
   * Use `{ mode: "external" }` to skip starting a local Worker entirely —
   * useful when an external dev server (e.g. one spawned via `Command.Dev`)
   * is serving the content this Worker would otherwise host.
   */
  dev?:
    | {
        /**
         * Run this Worker in `workerd` locally (the default).
         * @default "worker"
         */
        mode?: "worker";
        /**
         * Host the local dev server binds to.
         * @default "localhost"
         */
        host?: string;
        /**

         */
        port?: number;
        /**
         * When `true`, fail instead of falling back to another port if
         * {@link port} is already in use.
         * @default false

        strictPort?: boolean;

*
 * ```typescript
 * Effect.gen(function* () {
 *   // Phase 1: bind resources (runs at deploy time)
 *   const kv = yield* Cloudflare.KV.ReadWriteNamespace(MyKV);
 *
 *   return {
 *     // Phase 2: runtime handlers (runs on each request)
 *     fetch: Effect.gen(function* () {
 *       const value = yield* kv.get("key");
 *       return HttpServerResponse.text(value ?? "not found");
 *     }),
 *   };
 * })
 * ```
 *
 * There are three ways to define a Worker, from simplest to most
 * flexible. See the [Functions & Servers](/infrastructure-as-effects/functions-and-servers)
 * page for the full explanation.
 *
 * - **Async** — plain `async fetch` handler, no Effect runtime in the bundle.
 * - **Effect** — Effect implementation passed directly, single file.
 * - **Layer** — class and `.make()` in a single file; Rolldown tree-shakes `.make()` from consumers.
 * ### Protect with Access
 * Put Cloudflare Access in front of the Worker with the `access` prop —
 * unauthenticated requests are redirected to your team's login page, and
 * handlers read the authenticated identity from `ctx.access` via
 * `Cloudflare.Access.Context`. See the
 * [Protect a Worker with Access](/cloudflare/security/access) guide.
 *
 * **Example:** Dedicated application — per-Worker policies
 * The `{ policies }` form declares an Access application owned by this
 * Worker (namespaced under it as `<Worker>/Access`), created, updated,
 * and deleted with it:
 * ```typescript
 * export default Cloudflare.Worker(
 *   "Api",
 *   {
 *     main: import.meta.url,
 *     access: {
 *       policies: [
 *         { decision: "allow", include: [{ emailDomain: "example.com" }] },
 *       ],
 *     },
 *     // simulate the authenticated state under `alchemy dev`
 *     dev: { access: { aud: "dev", identity: { email: "dev@example.com" } } },
 *   },
 *   Effect.gen(function* () {
 *     return {
 *       fetch: Effect.gen(function* () {
 *         const access = yield* Cloudflare.Access.Context;
 *         const identity = yield* access!.getIdentity();
 *         return yield* HttpServerResponse.json({ email: identity?.email });
 *       }),
 *     };
 *   }),
 * );
 * ```
 *
 * **Example:** Shared application — one policy set, many Workers
 * Pass a `Cloudflare.Access.Application` directly to enroll into it.
 * Access policies are application-wide: every enrolled Worker is gated
 * by the same policy set.
 * ```typescript
 * const TeamOnly = Cloudflare.Access.Application("TeamOnly", {
 *   type: "self_hosted",
 *   policies: [
 *     { decision: "allow", include: [{ emailDomain: "example.com" }] },
 *   ],
 * });
 *
 * export default Cloudflare.Worker(
 *   "Api",
 *   { main: import.meta.url, access: TeamOnly },
 *   /* ... *​/
 * );
 * ```
 *
 * ### Async Workers
 * You don't have to use Effect for your runtime code. If you create
 * a Worker resource with `main` pointing at a file but provide no
 * `Effect.gen` implementation, Alchemy bundles and deploys that file
 * as-is. Your handler is a plain `async fetch` — no Effect runtime
 * is included in the bundle.
 *
 * Use the `env` prop to declare which resources, `Config` values,
 * and literal env vars are available at runtime, and
 * `Cloudflare.InferEnv` to extract a fully typed `env` object from
 * them.
 *
 * See the [Workers guide](/cloudflare/compute/workers)
 * for a comprehensive walkthrough of all binding types (R2, D1,
 * Durable Objects, Assets, and more).
 *
 * **Example:** Defining an async Worker in your stack
 * ```typescript
 * // alchemy.run.ts
 * const db = yield* Cloudflare.D1.Database("DB");
 * const bucket = yield* Cloudflare.R2.Bucket("Bucket");
 *
 * export type WorkerEnv = Cloudflare.InferEnv<typeof Worker>;
 *
 * export const Worker = Cloudflare.Worker("Worker", {
 *   main: "./src/worker.ts",
 *   env: { db, bucket },
 * });
 * ```
 *
 * **Example:** Writing the async handler
 * ```typescript
 * // src/worker.ts
 * import type { WorkerEnv } from "../alchemy.run.ts";
 *
 * export default {
 *   async fetch(request: Request, env: WorkerEnv) {
 *     if (request.method === "GET") {
 *       const object = await env.bucket.get("key");
 *       return new Response(object?.body ?? null);
 *     }
 *     return new Response("Not Found", { status: 404 });
 *   },
 * };
 * ```
 *
 * ### Python Workers
 * Point `main` at a `.py` file to deploy a
 * [Python Worker](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/languages/python/)
 * (open beta). There is no bundling step — the entry and every sibling
 * `.py` module upload as-is and are interpreted by Pyodide, and the
 * `python_workers` compatibility flag is added automatically. Like async
 * Workers, Python Workers take no inline Effect implementation; declare
 * bindings with the `env` prop and read them from `self.env` in Python.
 *
 * Dependencies come from `pyproject.toml` next to the entry: Alchemy
 * vendors `[project.dependencies]` with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)
 * against the Pyodide wheel index and uploads them under
 * `python_modules/`. If a `python_modules/` directory already exists
 * (e.g. produced by `pywrangler sync`), it is uploaded as-is and uv is
 * not invoked.
 *
 * See the [Python Workers guide](/cloudflare/compute/python-workers)
 * for the full walkthrough.
 *
 * **Example:** Defining a Python Worker in your stack
 * ```typescript
 * // alchemy.run.ts
 * const kv = yield* Cloudflare.KV.Namespace("Cache");
 *
 * export const Worker = Cloudflare.Worker("Worker", {
 *   main: "./src/worker.py",
 *   env: { CACHE: kv },
 * });
 * ```
 *
 * **Example:** Writing the Python handler
 * ```python
 * # src/worker.py
 * from workers import Response, WorkerEntrypoint
 *
 * class Default(WorkerEntrypoint):
 *     async def fetch(self, request):
 *         cached = await self.env.CACHE.get("greeting")
 *         return Response(cached or "Hello from Python!")
 * ```
 *
 * **Example:** Vendoring dependencies with pyproject.toml
 * ```toml
 * # src/pyproject.toml — vendored with uv on deploy
 * [project]
 * name = "my-worker"
 * version = "0.1.0"
 * requires-python = ">=3.13"
 * dependencies = ["humanize"]
 * ```
 *
 * ### Effect Workers
 * Pass the Effect implementation as the third argument. This is the
 * simplest Effect-based approach — everything lives in one file.
 * Convenient for standalone Workers that don't need to be referenced
 * by other Workers.
 *

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# The first-run walkthrough: gather the deployment's identity, generate the
# signing keypair, and write infra/.env.production with everything a deploy
# needs. The GitHub and Cloudflare console steps cannot be scripted, so the
# script prints them as checklists at the points where they matter. Safe to
# rerun: it refuses to overwrite an existing file without --force.
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

env_file="infra/.env.production"
if [ -e "${env_file}" ] && [ "${1:-}" != "--force" ]; then
    echo "cachet: ${env_file} already exists." >&2
    echo "cachet: rerun with \`just bootstrap -- --force\` to rebuild it." >&2
    exit 1
fi

preflight() {
    local missing=()
    command -v cargo >/dev/null 2>&1 || missing+=("cargo (run this inside \`nix develop\`)")
    command -v bun >/dev/null 2>&1 || missing+=("bun (run this inside \`nix develop\`)")

# Deploys. Staging follows every green ci run on main; production is manual
# behind the GitHub environment's reviewer gate. Both stages read their
# configuration from environment-scoped vars and secrets (same names as
# infra/.env.<stage> locally), never from repository-level config, so the
# two stages can diverge safely.
name: deploy

on:
  workflow_run:
    workflows: [ci]
    branches: [main]
    types: [completed]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      stage:
        description: The stage to deploy
        required: true
        type: choice
        options:
          - staging
          - production
        default: staging

concurrency:
  # why: one deploy per stage at a time, and never cancel a deploy in
  # flight; a half-updated stage is worse than a queued one.
  group: deploy-${{ github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && inputs.stage || 'staging' }}
  cancel-in-progress: false

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  staging:
    if: github.event_name == 'workflow_run' && github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'success'
    environment: staging
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env: &deploy_env
      CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN }}
      CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID: ${{ secrets.CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID }}
      CACHET_SIGNING_KEY: ${{ secrets.CACHET_SIGNING_KEY }}
      GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET }}
      CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST: ${{ vars.CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST }}
      CACHET_DEPLOY_ORGS: ${{ vars.CACHET_DEPLOY_ORGS }}
      CACHET_DEPLOY_ADMINS: ${{ vars.CACHET_DEPLOY_ADMINS }}
      CACHET_DEPLOY_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID: ${{ vars.CACHET_DEPLOY_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID }}
      CACHET_DEPLOY_AUDIENCE: ${{ vars.CACHET_DEPLOY_AUDIENCE }}
      CACHET_DEPLOY_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF: ${{ vars.CACHET_DEPLOY_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF }}
      CACHET_DEPLOY_DOMAIN: ${{ vars.CACHET_DEPLOY_DOMAIN }}
      CACHET_DEPLOY_UI_ORIGIN: ${{ vars.CACHET_DEPLOY_UI_ORIGIN }}

input.content:
# Deploying cachet

cachet deploys into your own Cloudflare account. One deployment serves one
or more GitHub orgs; stages (`staging`, `production`) are fully separate
sets of resources that share nothing. The deploy itself is one command
(`just deploy <stage>`); everything below is what surrounds it.

## Prerequisites

Bring these before the first deploy:

1. A Cloudflare account and an API token with Workers Scripts:Edit,
   Workers KV Storage:Edit, R2:Edit, Zone:Read, and Zone:DNS:Edit on the
   zone that will serve the cache. The account id comes from the
   dashboard's right-hand sidebar.
2. A zone in that account for the cache's custom domain (for example
   `cache.example.com`). Production attaches the domain at deploy time;
   skip the zone only if you will run production on workers.dev, in which
   case set `CACHET_DEPLOY_DOMAIN` to something public you own anyway:
   the host name doubles as the signing key's name and appears in every
   narinfo signature, so choose it once.
3. A GitHub org whose Actions runners will write to the cache and whose
   members will read from it.
4. A GitHub OAuth App in that org: homepage `https://<host>`, callback
   `https://<host>/_auth/callback`, Device Flow enabled. The callback URL
   is fixed by the host, so it can be created before anything deploys.
5. The list of GitHub logins that get admin rights (the GC report API).

## The first run

Run `nix develop`, then `just bootstrap`. It asks for the values above,
generates the signing keypair (`cachet keygen`), and writes
`infra/.env.production` at mode 0600. That file holds the signing secret
and the OAuth client secret; it is gitignored, and it is the canonical
local store for them. The printed public key is what laptops will trust.

Deploy with the Cloudflare credentials in the environment:

```
CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=... CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID=... just deploy production
```

The recipe builds the wasm bundle, installs the infra dependencies from
the lockfile, sources `infra/.env.production`, and runs the alchemy
stack: R2 bucket, KV namespace, the worker with its bindings, the
garbage collector's cron (`0 5 * * *`), and the custom domain. It is
idempotent: rerunning converges, it never duplicates.

## The configuration contract

`just deploy` reads `infra/.env.<stage>` (or exported equivalents).
These variables name the deployment:

| Variable | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST` | yes | The cache's host name; also the signing key's name prefix. |
| `CACHET_DEPLOY_ORGS` | yes | Comma-joined GitHub org slugs; nobody outside them authenticates. |
| `CACHET_DEPLOY_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` | yes | The OAuth App's client id. |
| `CACHET_DEPLOY_ADMINS` | yes | Comma-joined GitHub logins allowed on `/api/self/*`. |
| `CACHET_DEPLOY_AUDIENCE` | no | OIDC audience; default `cachet`. |
| `CACHET_DEPLOY_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF` | no | The ref allowed to renew leases; default `refs/heads/main`. |
| `CACHET_DEPLOY_DOMAIN` | no | Custom domain; production defaults to the host, other stages to none. |
| `CACHET_DEPLOY_UI_ORIGIN` | no | Browser login's redirect target; unset answers 204 instead. |
| `CACHET_DEPLOY_GC_GRACE_MS` | no | Grace override; staging defaults to 0, elsewhere 14 days. |
| `CACHET_SIGNING_KEY` | yes | The `<host>-1:<base64>` secret from bootstrap. |
| `GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` | yes | The OAuth App's client secret. |

## Staging

`just deploy staging` deploys the same stack as `cachet-staging-*` with
no custom domain and with the GC grace window zeroed, so a seeded object
is sweepable on the very next collector tick. Use it to rehearse changes:
deploy staging, exercise it, then `just deploy production`. Tear a stage
down with `just destroy <stage>`; alchemy asks before deleting.

## CI deploys

The `deploy` workflow runs staging automatically after a green `ci` on
main. Production is manual: Actions > deploy > Run workflow, choosing
`production`, and the run waits for the `production` environment's
reviewer approval. Configure the two GitHub environments with the same
variables the local file carries: `CACHET_DEPLOY_*` as environment
variables, `CACHET_SIGNING_KEY`, `GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET`,
`CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`, and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` as environment
secrets.

## Verifying a deployment

`curl https://<host>/api/public/config` answers the orgs, the host, the
OAuth client id, and the public key; the key must match what bootstrap
printed. Then on a laptop: install the CLI from the release page, run
`cachet login --cache-url https://<host>`, `cachet setup`, and
`cachet doctor`; every probe should print `ok`. The collector fires on
the cron, and its runs appear under `/api/self/gc-runs` for an admin.

## Rollback

Redeploy the previous commit: `git checkout <previous> && just deploy
<stage>` converges the stack to that state. The collector's grace window
protects cache content through it; leases and reports persist in the
bucket, which is stage-scoped, so a rollback never strands state.

## Key rotation

Rotate the signing key by running `cachet keygen --name <host>-2` (the
suffix increments), replacing `CACHET_SIGNING_KEY` in the env file and in
the CI secrets, and redeploying. Deployments with clients configured
before the rotation must add the new public key: `cachet setup`
refreshes the trusted key list from the deployment's public config on
re-run.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# The first-run walkthrough: gather the deployment's identity, generate the
# signing keypair, and write infra/.env.production with everything a deploy
# needs. The GitHub and Cloudflare console steps cannot be scripted, so the
# script prints them as checklists at the points where they matter. Safe to
# rerun: it refuses to overwrite an existing file without --force.
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

env_file="infra/.env.production"
if [ -e "${env_file}" ] && [ "${1:-}" != "--force" ]; then
  echo "cachet: ${env_file} already exists." >&2
  echo "cachet: rerun with \`just bootstrap -- --force\` to rebuild it." >&2
  exit 1
fi

preflight() {
  local missing=()
  command -v cargo >/dev/null 2>&1 || missing+=("cargo (run this inside nix develop)")
  command -v bun >/dev/null 2>&1 || missing+=("bun (run this inside nix develop)")
  if [ "${#missing[@]}" -gt 0 ]; then
    printf 'cachet: missing: %s\n' "${missing[@]}" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
}

# prompt <question> [default] — answers on stdout, so assign with $(prompt ...).
prompt() {
  local question="$1" default="${2:-}" suffix=""
  [ -n "${default}" ] && suffix=" [${default}]"
  printf '%s%s: ' "${question}" "${suffix}" >&2
  read -r answer
  printf '%s' "${answer:-${default}}"
}

preflight

CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST="$(prompt "Cache host (the public domain, e.g. cache.example.com)")"

cat >&2 <<CHECKLIST
cachet: bootstrap needs one GitHub OAuth App. In the GitHub org you will
serve, open Settings > Developer settings > OAuth Apps > New OAuth App:

    Application name:               cachet
    Homepage URL:                   https://${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST}
    Authorization callback URL:     https://${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST}/_auth/callback
    Enable Device Flow:             on

Then copy the app Client ID, generate a Client Secret, and have both ready
for the next prompts.
CHECKLIST

CACHET_DEPLOY_ORGS="$(prompt "GitHub org slug(s) to serve, comma-separated")"
CACHET_DEPLOY_ADMINS="$(prompt "Admin GitHub login(s), comma-separated")"
CACHET_DEPLOY_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID="$(prompt "OAuth App client id")"
GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET="$(prompt "OAuth App client secret")"
CACHET_DEPLOY_AUDIENCE="$(prompt "OIDC audience" "cachet")"
CACHET_DEPLOY_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF="$(prompt "Default branch ref" "refs/heads/main")"

echo "cachet: generating the signing keypair..."
keydir="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "${keydir}"' EXIT
cargo run -q -p cachet-cli -- keygen --name "${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST}-1" --out-dir "${keydir}" >/dev/null
signing_key="$(tr -d '\n' <"${keydir}/cachet-key.secret")"
public_key="$(tr -d '\n' <"${keydir}/cachet-key.public")"
rm -rf "${keydir}"
trap - EXIT

cat >"${env_file}.tmp" <<ENV
# cachet deployment configuration, written by just bootstrap.
# CACHET_SIGNING_KEY never leaves this file and a secret store; keep the
# file at 0600 and never commit it.
CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST=${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST}
CACHET_DEPLOY_ORGS=${CACHET_DEPLOY_ORGS}
CACHET_DEPLOY_ADMINS=${CACHET_DEPLOY_ADMINS}
CACHET_DEPLOY_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID=${CACHET_DEPLOY_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID}
CACHET_DEPLOY_AUDIENCE=${CACHET_DEPLOY_AUDIENCE}
CACHET_DEPLOY_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF=${CACHET_DEPLOY_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF}
GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET=${GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET}
CACHET_SIGNING_KEY=${signing_key}
# Optional: the future UI's origin for the browser login redirect.
#CACHET_DEPLOY_UI_ORIGIN=https://ui.example.com
ENV
chmod 600 "${env_file}.tmp"
mv "${env_file}.tmp" "${env_file}"

cat <<SUMMARY
cachet: wrote ${env_file} (0600).
cachet: the deployment's public key is:

    ${public_key}

cachet: next steps, in order:

    1. Point the zone running ${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST} at this Cloudflare
       account: the custom domain attaches at deploy time and the zone
       must already exist there.
    2. Deploy: CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=... CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID=... just deploy production
       The token needs Workers Scripts:Edit, Workers KV Storage:Edit,

    3. If GitHub let you set the callback URL only roughly, make sure it

       cachet setup
       cachet doctor
    5. In CI: uses: nox-systems/cachet/action@v1 with cache-url:
       https://${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST} and permissions id-token: write.

# Architecture Decision Records

Each ADR records one decision: the context that forced it, the decision itself, the
consequences accepted, and the alternatives weighed. ADRs are the durable home for the
why — [CLAUDE.md](../../CLAUDE.md) §7 requires one per architectural decision and fixes
the editorial split they sit on: the living docs ([`../contracts.md`](../contracts.md),
[`../design/architecture.md`](../design/architecture.md),
[`../testing/strategy.md`](../testing/strategy.md)) carry what the system does and are
sufficient on their own to act; the ADRs carry why it does it that way and are opened on
demand, pointed at from the docs by a `(rationale: ADR NNNN)` marker.

**Format:** a `# ADR NNNN — <title>` line, then a `Status`, `Date`, and `Context doc`
header, then the sections Context, Decision (numbered), Consequences, and Alternatives
considered, in that order. A new ADR takes the next number.

**Not auto-loaded.** The CLAUDE.md §10 import manifest excludes `docs/adr/`
([ADR 0014](0014-auto-loaded-doc-context.md)): loading sixteen records of why would crowd
out the current-truth docs and invert the editorial principle. ADRs are living — when a
decision evolves the ADR is rewritten in place and git holds the history; when a
new decision replaces an old one, the old ADR is deleted and every reference moved. There are
no dated amendments and no superseded tombstones.

| ADR | Title | Status | What it settles |
|---|---|---|---|
| [0001](0001-no-database-garbage-collection.md) | No database: the reference graph is the narinfos | Accepted | GC marks from per-project lease documents (`roots/{project}`) and walks a reference graph read from the bucket's own narinfos — each `References` field is the edge list — so the graph cannot drift from the objects. No database, no queues, no R2 event notifications |
| [0002](0002-writes-through-the-worker.md) | Writes go through the Worker | Accepted | Zero S3/R2 credentials exist anywhere: the Worker reaches R2 through its binding (a deploy-time capability, not key material) and clients authenticate *to the Worker*, so every write passes our validation — which is what makes NEVER-DANGLE enforceable at write time |
| [0003](0003-upstream-filter.md) | The upstream filter | Accepted | The action drops every candidate path `cache.nixos.org` already serves before staging a push, since `nix copy` checks presence only at the destination. The roots' own outputs are never filtered, and an upstream error includes the path (FAIL-TOWARD-REBUILD) |
| [0004](0004-client-side-signing.md) | Client-side signing | Accepted | NARs are signed by the client at build time and verified by every client against the public key in each repo's flake `nixConfig`. The signing key never enters the Worker: auth controls *access*, signatures control *trust* |
| [0005](0005-no-temp-credential-vending.md) | No temporary credential vending (a rejected design, recorded) | Accepted | A Worker route minting short-lived scoped R2 credentials for CI, rejected and recorded so it is not re-proposed: an in-job attacker already holds the OIDC token that would mint them, so it buys no threat reduction and reintroduces R2 key material |
| [0006](0006-hono-for-routing-jose-for-oidc.md) | `hono` for routing, `jose` for OIDC | Accepted | Two libraries, two scopes: `hono` (≥ 4.11.4) owns routing and error mapping at the edge only; `jose` owns JWT verification. `hono/jwk` is deliberately off the auth path, and `createLocalJWKSet` keeps the JWKS fetch and TTL policy ours — core is handed the parsed key set and the current time |
| [0007](0007-bun-toolchain-workerd-runtime.md) | Bun is the toolchain, workerd is the runtime | Accepted | Bun is the package manager, script runner, action bundler (`bun build --target=node`), and fast test lane — never a production runtime. The Worker runs on workerd; `vitest` and `wrangler` run under node |
| [0008](0008-determinate-nix-everywhere.md) | Determinate Nix everywhere | Accepted | One Nix distribution on laptops and CI. Because Determinate manages `/etc/nix/nix.conf`, our settings live in `/etc/nix/nix.custom.conf` — which is why `cache-login` writes there. Vendor independence lives in the artifacts, not the runtime |
| [0009](0009-kind-not-k3d.md) | kind, not k3d (and why cachet needs neither) | Accepted | The org-level local-Kubernetes decision recorded for inheritance — kind's upstream components and real etcd over k3s/k3d's substitutions, version-pinned in a checked-in ctlptl `cluster.yaml` — and the explicit note that **cachet needs no cluster** |
| [0010](0010-pure-core-no-sims.md) | A pure core, and no simulators | Accepted | `src/core/` is pure functions taking plain arguments (`nowMs`, a parsed JWKS document) and narrow callbacks; `src/worker.ts` plus a thin `src/real/` do all the I/O. Nothing hand-written stands in for R2 or the Cache API — miniflare already ships both — and the depth goes to OIDC verification and the constant-time token comparison instead |
| [0011](0011-two-lane-test-split.md) | The two-lane test split | Accepted | The fast lane runs the pure functions under `bun test`, exhaustively and sub-second; the truth lane runs every route inside actual workerd against real miniflare-backed R2 and Cache API, and is the only place I/O behaviour is proven |
| [0012](0012-edge-cache-generation.md) | The edge-cache generation | Accepted | Object cache keys embed a monotonic generation persisted as `meta/generation` and resolved through the edge cache on a 60-second TTL, so long `immutable` TTLs are safe and a destructive sweep converges every PoP within a hard bound — no purge credentials anywhere |
| [0013](0013-deployment-identity-is-configuration.md) | Deployment identity is configuration, never source | Accepted | The cache hostname, the accepted `repository_owner`, the OIDC audience, and the default-branch ref are configuration — Worker vars, action input defaults, `nixConfig`, recipe arguments — never source literals. Non-production test fixtures make the ban self-enforcing |
| [0014](0014-auto-loaded-doc-context.md) | Auto-loaded documentation context (the CLAUDE.md import manifest) | Accepted | A flat `@`-import manifest loads the README and every non-ADR doc into every session; `scripts/check-doc-manifest.sh` gates completeness, exactly-once, and dead imports. ADRs stay out: they hold the *why* and are read on demand |
| [0015](0015-lease-read-routes-and-verifier.md) | The lease read routes and the verifier | Accepted | Adds `GET /roots` and `GET /roots/{project}` under read auth, plus optional lease provenance, so the verifier can rebuild what the leases pin with substitution disabled and compare — the only mechanism that detects an attacker who was inside CI |
| [0016](0016-flake-is-the-interface.md) | The flake is the interface | Accepted | `flake.nix` + `flake.lock` are the whole interface: the dev shell holds every tool and CI runs `nix develop -c just <verb>`. Two carve-outs recorded — no Tilt/kind/ctlptl/services-flake, and the bun and vitest lanes are not `nix flake check` derivations |

# ADR 0001 — Server-side signing, verify-then-sign

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-21
- **Context doc:** [../../CLAUDE.md](../../CLAUDE.md) §1, §7

## Context

Nix's trust model for binary caches is not transport trust. A narinfo
carries a `Sig` field: a detached ed25519 signature, labelled with a key
name, over a fingerprint composed from the store path, the NAR hash, the
NAR size, and the sorted references. A substituting client recomputes
the fingerprint and verifies the signature against its configured
trusted public keys; a failure means build-from-source, quietly. TLS and
authentication decide who may fetch, not what may be believed.

Someone who can place narinfos that clients trust can execute code on
every machine that substitutes from the cache. The previous cachet
deployment signed client-side: CI runners held the org's signing key as
a GitHub secret, and every job that could read the secret could mint
trust. Runners are shared, caches are sticky, and the key's disclosure
radius was every workflow in every repo in the org.

## Decision

1. The server holds the only signing key, as a Workers secret binding
   provisioned at deploy time. Clients upload unsigned narinfos staging
   through `nix copy` to a file:// destination without a secret key.
2. The worker signs a narinfo only after verifying its bytes: the
   store-path grammar, the NAR's presence in the bucket, the declared
   `NarHash` and `NarSize` recomputed against the stored object. The
   verified value is a distinct type the signing path requires, so an
   unverified narinfo cannot reach the signature by construction.
3. The narinfo's key name is the deployment's host with a numeric
   suffix (`<host>-1`), which makes rotation a redeploy and clients
   learn the public half from the deployment's public config document.

## Consequences

The trust radius of the signing key is the worker's secret binding and
the operator's deploy environment. A stolen OIDC token can upload
paths, but the uploaded narinfo must pass byte verification against the
NAR it names before it is signed; forgery requires defeating the
verification, not just the credential. The public config document is
the single source for the key clients trust, so rotation is one
redeploy with an incremented suffix rather than an org-wide keyswap
cable-pull. The cost is strictness: a wrong hash or size in an uploaded
narinfo is a hard 400, and pushes must stage exact bytes, which the
push pipeline does by hashing nothing itself and letting the server
check.

## Alternatives considered

Client-side signing (the previous deployment) keeps the worker simple
and puts the verification burden on consumers, at the price of the key
material described above; rejected. Signing an unverified document
server-side is strictly worse than either, since it turns a
configuration mistake into trusted poison; rejected.

# ADR 0002 — OIDC writes, device-flow laptop reads, browser OAuth for the UI

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-21
- **Context doc:** [../../CLAUDE.md](../../CLAUDE.md) §1; [../../SECURITY.md](../../SECURITY.md)

## Context

Three populations touch the cache with different powers. CI jobs push:
they run inside GitHub-hosted runners that can prove platform identity.
Laptops read: people on machines they own, whose trust is their GitHub
membership. Browsers read for a future UI: same people, over the web.
One credential type for all three was the previous deployment's answer
(a shared read token in a vault), and it failed the test of a
replacement: a shared token cannot be revoked per person, and every
person who leaves the org is a race against a rotated distribution.

## Decision

1. Writes accept GitHub OIDC tokens only: RS256 signatures verified
   against GitHub's published JWKS with a pinned algorithm and exact
   `iss`/`aud` checks, `repository_owner` against the deployment's org
   list, a bounded staleness on `iat`, and `exp` against the request
   clock. The token is the write credential; nothing else signs
   anything.
2. Laptops authenticate through GitHub's device flow, run by the CLI
   against github.com directly. The worker never participates in the
   flow; it validates the resulting user token per request by calling
   `/user` and an org-membership endpoint, caching the verdict in KV
   (600s for allow, 60s for deny). The token is personal, stored 0600
   on the laptop, and revocable at github.com.
3. Browsers use the OAuth code flow against the same worker:
   `/_auth/login` stores a one-shot state record, `/_auth/callback`
   exchanges the code server-side, checks org membership, and sets an
   HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite=Lax session cookie; `/logout` deletes the
   session. State records are consumed on use.
4. CI jobs read with the same OIDC credential they write with: a worker
   that sees a three-segment base64url token dispatches it to the
   write-path verifier instead of the user-token path, so runners need
   no second credential for substitution.

## Consequences

Each credential is personal and dies with its holder's org membership
(at most one verdict TTL late). Revoking a laptop means revoking one
GitHub account, not redistributing a secret. The device flow works on
headless machines. The KV verdict cache bounds GitHub API load and
defines the revocation window explicitly; administrators read it from
the OpenAPI-facing docs rather than inferring it.

## Alternatives considered

A shared pre-shared token (the old design): fails per-person
revocation; rejected. Fine-grained PATs distributed by the operator:
same distribution problem with extra bookkeeping; rejected. Requiring
OIDC for reads too, issued through a vending endpoint: adds a moving
part whose only customer is the laptop case the device flow already
serves; rejected.

# ADR 0003 — KV holds verdicts, sessions, and OAuth state only

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-21
- **Context doc:** [../../CLAUDE.md](../../CLAUDE.md) §1

## Context

Cloudflare gives a Workers deployment three obvious stores: R2 (object
storage, strong consistency, generous sizes), KV (globally replicated
key-value, eventually consistent, small values), and platform caches.
Narinfos, NARs, leases, upload records, GC cursors, and GC reports all
want durability and exact reads, which is R2's contract. Auth answers
want speed at the edge and short lives, which is KV's. The previous
deployment put no data in KV at all; the new auth design (ADR 0002) has
two places where a cached answer is the difference between a hot path
and a GitHub API call per request.

## Decision

1. R2 is the only cache-data store: object bytes and every worker-owned
   document (leases, upload records, GC cursors, GC reports, the
   generation marker) live there.
2. KV holds exactly three document kinds: token-validation verdicts
   (the `/user` plus org-membership answer, 600s allow TTL, 60s deny),
   browser sessions (14-day TTL), and OAuth state records (10-minute
   TTL, single-use).
3. Every KV document carries its own TTL; nothing in KV is expected to
   be true later than its TTL, and loss of the namespace degrades auth
   to the uncached path rather than breaking it.

## Consequences

The set of possible consistency bugs halves: every correctness-critical
read goes to a strongly-consistent store, and every KV answer is the
one the system would compute again anyway. The revocation window for a
GitHub-side change (membership removed, token revoked) is the verdict
TTL, documented rather than accidental. KV's eventual consistency never
lurks in GC or lease decisions.

## Alternatives considered

R2 for verdicts too: workable but pays R2's per-read latency on every
authenticated read and muddies the inventory enumeration with auth
documents; rejected. No KV at all (the old deployment): the per-request
GitHub API calls would rate-limit real usage; rejected. Durable Objects
for sessions: stronger than needed, and a single-writer object per
session buys nothing for a read-mostly session; rejected.

# ADR 0004 — The crypto set: sha2, ed25519-dalek, ruzstd, WebCrypto RS256

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-21
- **Context doc:** [../../CLAUDE.md](../../CLAUDE.md) §5; [../../deny.toml](../../deny.toml)

## Context

The worker compiles to wasm32-unknown-unknown, a target with no native
crypto libraries and no OpenSSL. The common Rust accelerator crates
(aws-lc-rs, ring's build, C zstd) embed C or assembly and do not build
for it. Meanwhile the native crates (push, CLI) need TLS on hosts, and
rustls's remaining provider choices are ring and aws-lc. One blanket
rule cannot serve both constraints, so the rule needs teeth in each
direction.

## Decision

1. The worker's cryptography is the pure-Rust, wasm-provable set:
   `sha2` for hashing, `ed25519-dalek` for signing, `ruzstd` for
   decompression.
2. RS256 verification (GitHub OIDC tokens) uses WebCrypto through the
   Workers runtime ({jsrs256}): workerd performs the signature math, so
   no RSA implementation ships in the wasm bundle at all. The `rsa`
   crate exists for host-side and test verification only.
3. The native crates bind TLS through reqwest's rustls feature, whose
   provider is `ring`. deny.toml bans `ring` workspace-wide except
   through the `rustls`/`rustls-webpki` wrappers, so a new dependency
   path to ring fails the gate; the wasm-hygiene scan of the shipped
   bundle is the independent backstop.
4. Entropy at the worker edge comes from the runtime's `getrandom` with
   the JS backend; host-side it is the OS. Secrets are zeroized where
   the type permits it, and the signing key exists only inside the
   secret-binding read that the signing path performs.

## Consequences

The supply-chain surface on the wasm side is auditable in one
read: four names, all pure Rust. deny.toml plus the bundle scan make
the wasm ban mechanical rather than aspirational. The native exception
is written down exactly where it is enforced, so a later contributor
reads the rule and the reason in the same place.

## Alternatives considered

`rustls` with aws-lc as the native provider: aws-lc ships C code with
its own build graph for no TLS benefit on the targets we support;
rejected. A single rust-builder for both targets with ring enabled
both ways: ring does not build for wasm32-unknown-unknown; impossible,
not rejected. Verifying RS256 in pure Rust inside the worker (rsa
crate): an unnecessary big-integer dependency in the bundle when the
runtime already verifies; rejected.

{jsrs256}
