<result>Research complete. Findings below, verified against current docs (August 2026).

---

## 1. How respected self-hosted projects stage config and secrets

**The dominant pattern: `.env` file sitting next to the compose/stack definition, inside the checkout, gitignored.** Every one of the surveyed Docker-world projects does this. The outliers that keep config *outside* the checkout are MinIO (`/etc`) and n8n (`~/.n8n`).

- **PocketBase** — single binary; config is flags + env vars; a 32-char `PB_ENCRYPTION_KEY` env var referenced by `--encryptionEnv` encrypts settings that otherwise sit as plain JSON in the SQLite DB. Deployment is rsync of one directory; recovery = restore `pb_data/` (manual copy, or built-in ZIP backups to local/S3). Docs: https://pocketbase.io/docs/going-to-production/
- **Umami** — `.env` with `DATABASE_URL` + `APP_SECRET` (`openssl rand -hex 32`); upgrade is `git pull && pnpm install && pnpm build` or `docker pull && docker compose up -d`. State lives in Postgres, so losing the `.env` costs only the APP_SECRET (invalidates tokens). Docs: https://umami.is/docs/environment-variables, https://umami.is/docs/install, https://docs.umami.is/docs/updates
- **Supabase self-hosting** — clone the repo, copy `docker/.env.example` to `docker/.env`, run `utils/generate-keys.sh` + `utils/add-new-auth-keys.sh` to fill secrets. `update.sh` does a three-way merge over your files on upgrade (your `.env` survives by virtue of the merge; `reset.sh` backs it up to `.env.old`). Docs explicitly say "all secrets are in the `.env` file by default; we strongly recommend using a secrets manager in production" (Doppler, Infisical, Vault, cloud secret managers). Losing the `.env` = losing the JWT secret lineage; keys must be regenerated. Docs: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/self-hosting/docker, env reference: https://github.com/supabase/supabase/blob/master/docker/CONFIG.md
- **Infisical (self-hosted)** — same shape: `.env` with `ENCRYPTION_KEY` (16-byte hex), `AUTH_SECRET` (32-byte base64), `DB_CONNECTION_URI`, `REDIS_URL`. Docs give the exact `openssl rand` commands they expect operators to paste. https://infisical.com/docs/self-hosting/configuration/envars
- **Documenso** — `cp .env.example .env`; docs ship a required-var table (`NEXTAUTH_SECRET`, two encryption keys, DB URL, SMTP). https://docs.documenso.com/docs/self-hosting/configuration/environment, https://docs.documenso.com/docs/self-hosting/deployment/manual
- **MinIO** — the strongest "config outside the checkout" example: systemd unit loads `EnvironmentFile=/etc/default/minio`, which only points at the real config file `/etc/minio/config.env` via `MINIO_CONFIG_ENV_FILE`; upgrade is a package replacement that never touches `/etc`. https://github.com/minio/minio-service/blob/master/linux-systemd/README.md, https://github.com/minio/minio-service/blob/master/linux-systemd/minio.service
- **n8n** — home-dir custody: first launch generates a credential-encryption key into `~/.n8n/config`; env var `N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (and a `_FILE` suffix variant) override only if the file doesn't already hold a key. Losing that file means stored credentials are unrecoverable — the community thread confirms changing the supply mechanism post-hoc resets the instance. https://docs.n8n.io/deploy/host-n8n/configure-n8n/basic-configuration/configuration-examples/set-a-custom-encryption-key, https://community.n8n.io/t/274522
- **Tailscale operator** — placeholders in `deploy/manifests/operator.yaml` (`client_id`/`client_secret` go into a K8s Secret `operator-oauth`); Helm values create the Secret for you. tsnet device state itself is stored in a Secret. https://tailscale.com/docs/kubernetes-operator/install-operator, https://github.com/tailscale/tailscale/blob/main/cmd/k8s-operator/deploy/manifests/operator.yaml

**Common thread for recovery:** the state store (Postgres, `pb_data`, Cloudflare account resources) survives config loss; what dies is minted secrets, which every project treats as re-issuable by rerunning the generation step. None of them treat the clone as precious — but their `.env` *does* live in the clone, so "disposable clone" is only half-achieved by the mainstream pattern.

## 2. The "config outside the clone" pattern — tool status, 2026

- **XDG / home-dir custody** is the CLI-world standard (see §4) and the server-world precedent is MinIO's `/etc`. Nobody in the Docker cohort bothers because the compose file pins them to a directory.
- **dotenvx** — active and credible. secp256k1; encrypted `.env` is commit-safe, `.env.keys` is the uncommitted crown jewel; CI injects `DOTENV_PRIVATE_KEY=... dotenvx run -- cmd`; documents 1Password/Bitwarden sourcing (`$(op read ...)`) for the private key. Newer `dotenvx armor up` stores keys off-device. https://dotenvx.com/docs/env-keys-file, https://dotenvx.com/docs/cli/encrypt-fk
- **sops + age** — CNCF Sandbox (healthy, growing contributors); age is the recommended backend; `sops exec-env` injects decrypted env into a command — a clean fit for "optional vault" glue. https://www.cncf.io/projects/sops/, https://getsops.io/
- **ejson (Shopify)** — **not archived** (search results claiming otherwise are stale); last release v1.5.4 Feb 2025, commits into 2026. Viable but a smaller ecosystem than sops/dotenvx. https://github.com/Shopify/ejson
- **varlock** (2025-era, dmno-dev) — `.env.schema` with `@required @sensitive @type=string(...)` decorators, `varlock scan` leak detection; the most credible current answer to "env contract validation as code." https://varlock.dev/guides/schema/, https://varlock.dev/env-spec/overview/, https://github.com/dmno-dev/varlock
- For a one-worker deployment the right baseline is **plain dotenv-format file at 0600 in an XDG path** (zero tooling), with dotenvx/sops/op/infisical as opt-in sourcing layers — they all converge on "decrypt → export env → run command," so anything reading env vars supports all four for free.

## 3. Programmatic deployments (Pulumi-like / alchemy)

- **Pulumi:** `pulumi new` scaffolds from templates; per-stack `Pulumi.<stack>.yaml` is *committed to the consumer's repo* with secrets encrypted inline (`secretsprovider` + `encryptedkey` fields). Local/object-store backends default to the `passphrase` provider — no Pulumi Cloud required; `--secrets-provider` overrides to KMS/Vault. ESC exists for shared config but is Pulumi-Cloud-dependent. So Pulumi's answer to "custody" is: encrypted-in-your-repo, key elsewhere. https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/cli/commands/pulumi_new/, https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/concepts/secrets/, https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/concepts/projects/stack-settings-file/, https://www.pulumi.com/docs/esc/concepts/environments/
- **Alchemy (v2, what cachet uses):** secrets come from the **deployer's process environment** (conventionally a `.env` loaded by the operator); `Config.redacted("NAME")` binds as Cloudflare `secret_text` regardless of constructor. Local state lives in `.alchemy/` (gitignored, stack+stage-scoped JSON); secrets in state are encrypted with a password passed at init (e.g. `SECRET_PASSPHRASE`); losing the password or state doesn't lose the deployed resources since the names are deterministic. `alchemy create` scaffolds consumer projects from templates. **There is no alchemy-native custody convention beyond "env of whoever runs the deploy" — cachet must define it.** https://alchemy.run/concepts/secrets/, https://alchemy.run/concepts/state/, https://alchemy.run/concepts/secret, https://alchemy.run/concepts/cli

## 4. Secrets-entry UX convergence in good CLIs

All five converged on the same shape: **interactive auth → write 0600/keystore entry under a home/XDG path → env var is the CI override.**

- **gh:** OS keyring (macOS Keychain / Secret Service / wincred), fallback plaintext `~/.config/gh/hosts.yml`; `GH_TOKEN` for CI. https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_auth_login, https://github.com/cli/cli/pull/7023
- **wrangler:** `~/.config/.wrangler/config/default.toml` (XDG-aware, mode 0600); as of **June 2026**, opt-in `--use-keyring` stores an AES-256-GCM file with the key in the OS keychain; `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` is the CI path; `wrangler whoami` reports where credentials live. https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/wrangler/commands/general/, https://developers.cloudflare.com/changelog/post/2026-06-03-wrangler-keyring-credential-storage/
- **flyctl:** `~/.fly/config.yml` `access_token:`; `FLY_ACCESS_TOKEN` wins (and gets persisted). https://github.com/superfly/flyctl/blob/master/internal/config/config.go
- **supabase CLI:** `~/.supabase/access-token` (newer versions keyring); `SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN` is the documented CI mechanism. https://supabase.com/docs/reference/cli/introduction
- **stripe CLI:** `~/.config/stripe/config.toml`, and notably `stripe login` mints a **restricted key (`rk_…`)** — the stored credential is minimally-scoped by construction; `STRIPE_API_KEY` env override. https://docs.stripe.com/stripe-cli/keys, https://docs.stripe.com/cli/config

Two takeaways: XDG paths with 0600 are the uncontroversial baseline (nobody forces a password manager); scope-minimizing the stored credential (stripe) is the differentiator — cachet's bootstrap already demands a *scoped* Cloudflare API token list in DEPLOY.md, which is the right instinct.

## 5. Env-contract docs and token verification at bootstrap

- **Contract-as-docs:** Supabase's `docker/CONFIG.md` (aggregated var reference), Documenso's and Infisical's required-var tables with exact generation commands. Contract-as-code: varlock's `.env.schema`.
- **Verification endpoints that exist and are cheap:**
  - Cloudflare: `GET /client/v4/user/tokens/verify` returns `{id, status: active|disabled|expired, expires_on}` — the canonical bootstrap probe. https://developers.cloudflare.com/api/resources/user/subresources/tokens/methods/verify/
  - GitHub OAuth app: `POST /applications/{client_id}/token` (basic auth with client_id/client_secret) checks a token belongs to that app (404 if not). https://docs.github.com/en/rest/apps/oauth-applications
  - GitHub scopes surface in `X-OAuth-Scopes` response headers (how `gh auth status` shows them).
  - Note: a GitHub OAuth *client secret* cannot be verified without running an OAuth flow; bootstrap can only format-check it and verify the client_id.

---

## Recommended custody model for cachet

**1. Move the operator env file out of the clone.** Canonical location `${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-~/.config}/cachet/deploy/<stage>.env`, mode 0600, written by `just bootstrap` instead of today's `infra/.env.production`. Precedence, matching every CLI surveyed: process env > `$CACHET_DEPLOY_CONFIG` (explicit file path) > XDG file > in-clone `infra/.env.<stage>` with a deprecation warning. `just deploy`/`just destroy` source through that chain (today they only check `infra/.env.<stage>` — justfile lines 111–136). Clone deletion then destroys only code and alchemy local state; `infra/.alchemy` state loss is non-catastrophic because alchemy resource names are deterministic and re-converges, and the secrets themselves live in the XDG file and as Cloudflare bindings.

**2. # Operator-side CI/CD for OSS deployables on GitHub Actions (verified August 2026)

## 1. Reusable workflows (`workflow_call`) as the operator-facing deploy product

**Mechanics, verified against docs.github.com** ([Reuse workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/reuse-automations/reuse-workflows), [Workflow syntax](https://docs.github.com/actions/using-workflows/workflow-syntax-for-github-actions)):

- Caller references: `uses: {owner}/{repo}/.github/workflows/{file}@{ref}` — works cross-org for **public** repos. `{ref}` may be a tag, branch, or **full SHA**; docs: "Using the commit SHA is the safest option for stability and security." The workflow version executed is the one at that ref.
- Secrets are **never auto-passed** cross-boundary. The caller passes them explicitly (`secrets: { name: ${{ secrets.X }} }`) or with `secrets: inherit`. A caller passing an undeclared secret is an error. Documented quirk that matters for cachet: `secrets: inherit` is designed for same-org/same-enterprise calls and **fails at evaluation time for cross-org calls** even when the names exist ([diogenes-project/diogenes#221](https://github.com/diogenes-project/diogenes/issues/221), [actions/runner#3206](https://github.com/actions/runner/issues/3206), [github/docs#44458](https://github.com/github/docs/issues/44458)). Since operators live outside the nox-systems org, the upstream workflow must declare every secret by name and operators must map them explicitly.
- **Environment protection rules resolve against the caller repo.** The called workflow can't take `environment` at `on.workflow_call`, but its jobs can set `environment: ${{ inputs.stage }}` (expressions are allowed); required reviewers on the *operator's* "production" environment then gate the job, including secret access ([Deploying with environments](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/deployments-and-environments), [actions/runner#4453](https://github.com/actions/runner/issues/4453)). Caveat: environment-scoped secrets resolve inside the called workflow only when the caller also passes them (`secrets: inherit` being broken cross-org, operators must map env secrets explicitly by name).
- **Permissions flow down, never up**: "permissions can only be maintained or reduced" through the call chain. For OIDC, the *caller job* must grant `permissions: id-token: write`; a called workflow can't self-grant it ([changelog 2023-06-15](https://github.blog/changelog/2023-06-15-github-actions-securing-openid-connect-oidc-token-permissions-in-reusable-workflows/), [josh-ops guide](https://josh-ops.com/posts/github-actions-oidc-reusable-workflows/)). The tolerable side effect: **OIDC subject claims describe the caller repo and environment** (`repo:operator/repo:environment:production`), so cloud trust policies bound to the operator repo still hold even though the workflow code is upstream.
- Nesting max 10 levels, no loops; matrix can fan out calls; outputs return via `needs.<job>.outputs`.
- The called workflow's `GITHUB_TOKEN` is the **caller's repo token**; a public upstream repo can still be re-checked-out inside it at any ref via `actions/checkout` with `repository:`/`ref:`.

**Caller-side shape (pattern A, what cachet operators would write):**

```yaml
# operator repo: .github/workflows/cachet-deploy.yml
name: deploy cachet
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      tag: { description: "cachet release tag", default: "v1.4.2" }
      stage: { description: "staging or production", default: "staging" }
  schedule: [ { cron: "17 4 * * 1" } ]   # weekly drift check, optional

jobs:
  deploy:
    permissions:
      contents: read          # job-level least privilege, nothing else needed
    uses: nox-systems/cachet/.github/workflows/operator-deploy.yml@v1.4.2
    with:
      stage: ${{ inputs.stage || 'staging' }}
      cachet-tag: ${{ inputs.tag || 'v1.4.2' }}
    secrets:
      CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN }}
      CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID: ${{ secrets.CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID }}
      CACHET_SIGNING_KEY: ${{ secrets.CACHET_SIGNING_KEY }}
      GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET }}
```

**Production examples doing this in the wild:**
- `slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator` — the marquee cross-org reusable workflow; its docs and open issues are the best existing study of tag-vs-SHA pinning friction ([issue #4216](https://github.com/slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator/issues/4216), [issue #4440](https://github.com/slsa-framework/slsa-github-generator/issues/4440): SHA-pinning callers broke their release-asset downloading and even violated GitHub's own "require SHA-pinned actions" org policy, because the workflow's *internal* `uses:` lines weren't SHA-pinned).
- [celo-org/reusable-workflows](https://github.com/celo-org/reusable-workflows) — versioned `@v3.0.0` tags, per-caller least-privilege `permissions:` blocks, optional `environment` input for deploy gating.
- [aws-samples/aws-terraform-reusable-workflow](https://github.com/aws-samples/aws-terraform-reusable-workflow/blob/main/.github/workflows/terraform-reusable.yml) — deploy/destroy as a callable product with `id-token: write` OIDC.
- [oslokommune/reusable-terraform-pr-plan](https://github.com/oslokommune/reusable-terraform-pr-plan) — municipal org running operator repos against a central workflow.
- The chrischall/setlist-mcp [deploy-at-release-tag pattern](https://github.com/chrischall/setlist-mcp/pull/70) shows the "deploy the released tag, not main" discipline.

## 2. Composite/JS action as the whole-deploy unit

Mechanics ([metadata syntax](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/metadata-syntax), [composite secrets](https://latchkey.dev/learn/github-actions/github-actions-composite-action-cannot-access-secrets), [nested uses](https://latchkey.dev/learn/github-actions/gha-composite-nested-uses-error)): a composite action **cannot read `secrets.*` at all** — the operator must pass every secret as a `with:` input, which is more verbose but forces the contract to be explicit. Composite steps may themselves `uses:` other actions. Local `./` paths inside it resolve against the action repo, so the action must be fully self-contained.

**Caller-side shape (pattern B):**

```yaml
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production            # protection rules apply normally; job is the caller's own
    steps:
      - uses: nox-systems/cachet/deploy-action@v1
        with:
          stage: production
          cachet-tag: v1.4.2
        env:
          CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN }}
          CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID: ${{ secrets.CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID }}
          CACHET_SIGNING_KEY: ${{ secrets.CACHET_SIGNING_KEY }}
          GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET }}
```

Comparison to a reusable workflow as secret consumer: trust exposure is identical (upstream code runs with your secrets in both). The differences: an action keeps `environment:` on the operator's own job (reviewer gating is trivially unambiguous and env secret wiring has no inherit quirk), while a reusable workflow gives a full job graph, its own runner/OS choice, outputs, and isolates upstream's `permissions:` needs from the caller's jobs. The SLSA precedent suggests large security-conscious consumers prefer reusable workflows; every Cloudflare-adjacent OSS (cloudflare/wrangler-action, [BotCoder254/cloudflare-promoter](https://github.com/BotCoder254/cloudflare-promoter)) ships the action form. Note cachet already has precedent constraints: an action can't run `just`, so the deploy machinery must be invocable as `bun run deploy --stage X` (it already is — `infra/alchemy.run.ts`).

## 3. "No repo at all" options

- **Real answer: GitHub Actions always needs at least one repo** holding the caller workflow YAML. There is no scheduled/manual Actions run without a repo. The realistic floor is a tiny config repo with one workflow file, which doubles as the version-pin record (see §4).
- **Cloudflare Workers Builds** ([docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/ci-cd/builds/), [config](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/ci-cd/builds/configuration/)): connects a GitHub/GitLab repo the operator owns, builds on push to one **branch** (tags/releases not a trigger), deploy command is customizable but wrangler-shaped. Build image ([build-image docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/ci-cd/builds/build-image/)) is Ubuntu 24.04 with Node 22/24, Bun 1.2, Go, Python — **no Rust/cargo preinstalled**, and build variables/secrets are build-time only. For cachet that means building wasm in their CI container is possible but unsupported-feeling, and upgrades mean syncing code in the operator's clone — it fails the "bump a version input" requirement.
- **Deploy to Cloudflare button** ([docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/deploy-buttons/), [blog](https://blog.cloudflare.com/deploy-workers-applications-in-seconds/), [July 2025 changelog adding vars/secrets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/changelog/post/2025-07-01-workers-deploy-button-supports-environment-variables-and-secrets/)): one click clones the upstream repo into the operator's GitHub account as an independent copy (not a fork), provisions KV/R2/D1 from wrangler config, prompts for secrets, and wires Workers Builds. It's the best zero-friction Cloudflare-native story, but the clone is a snapshot: no upstream sync mechanism, so upgrades are manual git surgery. cachet's deploy path (`alchemy`, secret bindings, env-file contract, workers-rs build) doesn't fit the button's wrangler-deploy model without re-engineering.
- No workers-ci managed-runner equivalent replaces the operator CI requirement.

## 4. Version pinning, upgrade automation, and the supply-chain trust question

- **Dependabot** has officially updated reusable-workflow refs (tags *and* SHAs) since [March 2023](https://github.blog/changelog/2023-03-13-dependabot-updates-support-reusable-workflows-for-github-actions/): `package-ecosystem: "github-actions"` bumps both `uses:` actions and `owner/repo/.github/workflows/x.yml@ref` lines ([docs](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/how-tos/secure-your-supply-chain/secure-your-dependencies/auto-update-actions)). Known rough edge: exotic monorepo tag schemes break it ([dependabot-core#8451](https://github.com/dependabot/dependabot-core/issues/8451)); plain `repo/.github/workflows/x.yml@vX.Y.Z` is fine.
- **Renovate**'s github-actions manager updates `workflow_call` refs natively, including SHA pins with version comments (real-world: [sbaerlocher/.github](https://github.com/sbaerlocher/.github) pins by date tag, Renovate keeps it current).
- **Tag vs SHA**: GitHub docs say SHA is safest; OpenSSF Scorecard's Pinned-Dependencies check enforces SHA, and GitHub now offers an org policy to *require* full-length SHA pins. But SLSA's experience proves a reusable workflow whose internals aren't themselves fully SHA-pinned and whose release assets aren't resolvable from a bare SHA **fails outright** for SHA-pinning callers. Options: (a) ship SHA-compatible internals and let operators SHA-pin (also keep a semver tag in a trailing `# v1.4.2` comment so Dependabot/Renovate can still propose bumps), or (b) publish moving major tags (`@v1`) plus immutable patch tags and recommend patch tags. Choose deliberately and test the SHA path in cachet's own CI, since that is exactly the path security-reviewing customers will take.
- **What the upstream workflow can do with operator secrets**: everything — it runs arbitrary upstream code in a run that has been handed the operator's Cloudflare token, signing key, and OAuth secret. GitHub's documented mitigations ([secure use reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use)): job-level least-privilege `permissions:`, **protected environments with required reviewers** (a deploy to `production` stalls until a human approves, which also gates environment secret access), org-level allow-lists of permitted actions/workflows, and SHA pinning. cachet must document that operators should bind `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` to a **scoped token** (Workers Scripts:Edit + KV + R2 + zone rights for exactly one zone) because Cloudflare still has no OIDC for wrangler/alchemy deploys — [workers-sdk discussion #11434](https://github.com/cloudflare/workers-sdk/discussions/11434), [wrangler-action#402](https://github.com/cloudflare/wrangler-action/issues/402), community bridge [waigel/cf-oidc-proxy](https://github.com/waigel/cf-oidc-proxy).
- **2024–2026 practitioner material** on self-host CI without forking: the reusable-workflow-with-OIDC pattern is well covered ([josh-ops](https://josh-ops.com/posts/github-actions-oidc-reusable-workflows/), [cloudchronicles env secrets guide](https://cloudchronicles.blog/blog/Passing-Environment-Secrets-and-Variables-to-Reusable-Workflows-in-GitHub-Actions/)); Cloudflare-specific "others deploy my worker" writing concentrates on the Deploy Button route above, not reusable workflows.

## 5. Recommendation for cachet

**Support two operator shapes, both released per tag:**

**Shape 1 (primary): reusable workflow `nox-systems/cachet/.github/workflows/operator-deploy.yml`.** Exact `workflow_call` surface:

```yaml
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      cachet-tag: { required: true, type: string }        # release tag to deploy
      stage:      { required: true, type: string }        # staging | production | ...
    secrets:
      CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN:       { required: true }
      CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID:      { required: true }
      CACHET_SIGNING_KEY:         { required: true }
      GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET: { required: true }
```

Inside: jobs set `environment: ${{ inputs.stage }}` (operator reviewer gates apply), non-secret config (`CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST`, `CACHET_DEPLOY_ORGS`, `CACHET_DEPLOY_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID`, `CACHET_DEPLOY_ADMINS`, optional overrides) read from the operator's environment `vars` context — vars are not secret-bearing, so the cross-org explicit-secrets rule doesn't touch them. The workflow downloads the **prebuilt bundle for `inputs.cachet-tag`** (no Rust toolchain on the runner) and runs the packaged alchemy program with bun.

**Shape 2 (secondary): composite action `nox-systems/cachet/deploy-action@v1`** as a thin wrapper over the same bundle+alchemy invocation, for operators who want deploy as one step inside a larger workflow and for OIDC-free simplicity of operator-owned job environments. Same secret contract via `env:`.

**What the upstream release pipeline must emit** (this is the real repo change):
1. **A prebuilt worker bundle asset per tag** (`cachet-worker-<tag>.tar.gz`: `worker-build --release` output + `worker-build` metadata), produced in the existing `release.yml`, so no operator machine ever needs cargo/wasm tooling — mirrors cachet-cli's cargo-dist precedent in the same repo. The integration lane should consume this asset too, so the shipped artifact is the tested artifact.
2. **A packaged deploy program per tag**: `infra/` published as a versioned tarball (or tiny npm package) containing `alchemy.run.ts`, `bun.lock`, `package.json`, and the bundle's checksum; the reusable workflow fetches both assets from the GitHub release of `inputs.cachet-tag` (public repo, no token needed) and runs `bun install --frozen-lockfile && bun run deploy --stage "$STAGE"`.
3. **SHA-pinning hygiene inside the workflows themselves**: every internal `uses:` SHA-pinned (the SLSA failure mode), plus a checksum verification of the downloaded bundle.
4. **A `v1` moving tag policy** alongside immutable `v1.x.y` tags for Shape 2's action, and a documented operator quickstart: create repo, add one caller YAML, configure `staging`/`production` environments with reviewers, drop the four secrets and the `CACHET_DEPLOY_*` vars into them, run `workflow_dispatch`. Upgrades are a one-line tag bump that Dependabot or Renovate opens automatically.

Not recommended as supported paths: Workers Builds (branch-driven, no Rust image, upgrade-by-resync) and the Deploy Button (snapshot clone, no upgrade story) — at most, mention the button as an evaluation/demo on-ramp in DEPLOY.md once the bundle story exists.

The CI research is back, and it's decisive. Verified findings:

1. **Reusable workflows are the canonical answer for operators on Actions**: one caller repo with ~15 lines of YAML, `uses: nox-systems/cachet/.github/workflows/operator-deploy.yml@<tag>`, secrets passed explicitly by name. Cloudflare's own ecosystem ships this shape as a composite action; both are viable, and the research recommends supporting both over one shared machinery.
2. **The honest constraint nobody escapes**: any upstream workflow or action executes with the operator's Cloudflare token and signing key in hand — trust in us is structural, and the documented mitigations (protected environments, scoped tokens, SHA pinning) all live operator-side. Worth saying plainly in DEPLOY.md rather than pretending away.
3. **The Deploy Button and Workers Builds are poor fits** for cachet specifically (wrangler-shaped, snapshot clones with no upgrade story, no Rust toolchain in the build image) — they answer "hello world" but not "upgrade from v0.0.1 to v0.0.2 by bumping one input".
4. **The real upstream deliverable this creates**: releases must publish a *prebuilt worker bundle* and a *packaged infra program* per tag, so no operator machine ever builds wasm. That also hardens our own guarantee — the integration lane then tests the exact artifact operators deploy.

# 1. Deploy to Cloudflare Workers button

Sources: https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/deploy-buttons/ , https://developers.cloudflare.com/changelog/post/2025-04-08-deploy-to-cloudflare-button/ , https://blog.cloudflare.com/deploy-workers-applications-in-seconds/ , https://github.com/cloudflare/deploy.workers.cloudflare.com (the old implementation)

**What it does today.** The button is a link of the form `https://deploy.workers.cloudflare.com/?url=<public git repo URL>` (subdirectories work by pointing the URL at a subdirectory path, as the cloudflare/templates repo buttons do). Clicking it walks the user through a hosted setup app that (a) clones the source repo into a new repo on the user's GitHub or GitLab account, (b) shows one setup page where the user edits repository name, Worker name, and resource names, (c) parses the repo's Wrangler configuration file, provisions every detected binding (KV namespaces, D1 databases, R2 buckets, Hyperdrive, Vectorize, Secrets Store secrets, Durable Objects, Workers AI, Queues), and writes the new resource IDs back into the clone's wrangler config, and (d) connects the clone to Workers Builds so every push to the production branch rebuilds and redeploys, and PR branches get preview URLs posted back as comments. Builds run on Cloudflare infrastructure, not GitHub Actions; the user never creates an API token by hand. Custom build/deploy commands are pre-detected from package.json scripts and editable; the default deploy command is `npx wrangler deploy`.

**Secrets and config.** Secrets are declared by the template author in a `.dev.vars.example` or `.env.example` file (dotenv format); the setup app collects values for them. Ordinary vars live in `[vars]` in the wrangler config and are copied verbatim from the template. Authors can attach per-binding explanatory text through a `cloudflare.bindings` description map in package.json (markdown inline code/bold/italics/links supported). D1 migrations must run from the user's deploy script keyed by binding name so renamed databases still migrate.

**Constraints.** Workers applications only (no Pages); repos must be public and hosted on github.com or gitlab.com (no self-hosted Git hosts, no private repos); monorepos only if the app subdirectory is fully self-contained; one button per Worker. Resource detection reads only the Wrangler config, so an alchemy stack (which declares resources in TypeScript, not wrangler.jsonc) gets no provisioning benefit. There is no mechanism for typed prompts over arbitrary config values: the flow can ask for secrets from the example env file and clone static defaults for vars, but it cannot present a form for "your GitHub orgs, your admin list, your host name". Custom domains are not provisioned or prompted for. Updating later is ordinary git pull-from-upstream plus a push.

Historical note: the previous button implementation (github.com/cloudflare/deploy.workers.cloudflare.com) was a GitHub OAuth integration that injected a GitHub Actions workflow with `cloudflare/wrangler-action` and populated repo secrets; it was replaced in April 2025 by the Workers Builds flow above.

**Fit for cachet's surface (~10 vars, 2 secrets, 1 token).** Partial. The button removes token creation and resource provisioning, but the 10 non-secret vars would ship as static clone values requiring manual edits and a second push, the custom-domain step stays manual, and the whole flow presumes a wrangler-config app, which an alchemy project is not.

# 2. create-cloudflare (C3)

Sources: https://developers.cloudflare.com/pages/get-started/c3/ , https://github.com/cloudflare/workers-sdk/pull/4754 , create-cloudflare@2.10.0 release notes, https://github.com/cloudflare/templates

Yes, third-party repos can ship C3 templates: `npm create cloudflare@latest -- my-app -- --template user/repo` (also `user/repo/subdir`, `user/repo#branch`, `user/repo#commit`, `bitbucket:`, `gitlab:`, full URLs; `--category remote-template`). Templates are cloned with degit, and the minimum required contents are a package.json, a Wrangler configuration file, and a `src/` folder containing a worker script referenced from the Wrangler config. Cloudflare's own catalog lives in github.com/cloudflare/templates and is consumed the same way (`--template cloudflare/templates/<name>`).

Mechanics relevant to self-hosting: after cloning, C3 installs dependencies and asks whether to deploy (`--deploy`, default true), which runs an interactive Cloudflare sign-in and deploys with wrangler; `--no-deploy`, `-y` (`--accept-defaults`), `--lang`, `--git`, `--open` control the rest. C3's prompting system covers only its built-in categories (`--category`, `--type`, `--framework`); a remote template cannot define its own prompts for config values. There is no `experimentalRemote` in the current CLI surface: the docs page documents no experimental flags, and remote-template support has been a stable `--template` option since 2.10.0. The mechanism assumes wrangler: template validation requires a Wrangler config, and the deploy step is wrangler. For an alchemy project, C3 would add nothing over `git clone`.

# 3. Other first-party machinery

**Workers Builds (GA since Developer Week 2025, April).** https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/ci-cd/builds/ and https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/ci-cd/builds/configuration/ . Connect a Worker to GitHub or GitLab from the dashboard (Workers & Pages, Create application, Import a repository, or an existing Worker's Settings > Builds). Two-step pipeline: optional build command, deploy command defaulting to `npx wrangler deploy`; preview deployments use `npx wrangler versions upload` for non-production branches. "Autoconfig" detects frameworks for repos without a wrangler config and opens a configuration PR. Limitations: the Worker's name must exactly match the `name` in the wrangler config or the build fails; one repo per Worker; no preview URLs for Workers with Containers. No beta label on these pages now.

**Versions, gradual deployments, rollbacks.** https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/versions-and-deployments/ . A version captures bundled code, static assets, bindings, and compatibility settings (KV/R2/D1/DO contents are explicitly not versioned). `wrangler deploy` creates a version and deploys it to 100 percent in one step; `wrangler versions upload` and `wrangler versions deploy` decouple the two; `wrangler versions list` and `wrangler deployments list` show the 100 most recent of each. Rollbacks revert to a previously deployed version; gradual deployments split traffic between two versions with optional version affinity. No beta designation on the docs page.

**Secrets Store (open beta, not GA).** https://developers.cloudflare.com/secrets-store/ and https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/wrangler/commands/secrets-store/ . Account-level secret store, one store per account, 100-secret cap during open beta. Bound to Workers through a `secrets_store_secrets` binding with `binding`, `store_id`, `secret_name` fields. CLI: `npx wrangler secrets-store secret create [STORE-ID] --name <NAME> --scopes workers --remote` with an interactive value prompt (the `--remote` flag is required for production operations; local mode is the default).

**workers-ci.** No wrangler feature by that name exists. The closest first-party artifact is github.com/cloudflare/ci, the `@cloudflare/ci` package, a Cloudflare-native CI engine built on Workflows and Sandbox: pipelines are TypeScript code you deploy as a Worker, requiring `nodejs_compat`. It is extremely early: 3 commits, no releases, no GA/beta label beyond its README caveats (raw logs not secret-redacted, runner commands must be idempotent under Workflow retries). Community-stage, not a product; not a deployment-UX tool for consumers.

**Templates catalog.** github.com/cloudflare/templates is the only official catalog, consumed by C3 and by deploy buttons; there is no documented third-party submission or gallery admission process.

# 4. Real OSS projects on Workers and how they present deployment

**R2-Explorer**, github.com/G4brym/R2-Explorer (docs at r2explorer.com). The README carries a working Deploy to Cloudflare button pointing at a subdirectory of the official templates repo: `https://deploy.workers.cloudflare.com/?url=https://github.com/cloudflare/templates/tree/main/r2-explorer-template`. It also documents three installation methods ("GitHub Action (Recommended)", "Cloudflare CLI" via create-cloudflare, template repository) and runs basic-auth/Access config through documented steps. This is the most polished "Cloudflare-native" distribution in the sample.

**Counterscale** (self-hosted web analytics), github.com/benvinegar/counterscale. No button, no clone. The flow is a purpose-built interactive installer: `npx wrangler login`, then `npx @counterscale/cli@latest install`, which prompts for a Cloudflare API token (minimum `Account.Account Analytics` permission) and an optional dashboard password, then deploys. Upgrades are re-running the installer with no new token; custom domains are a follow-on wrangler step. This is the homebrew-CLI pattern: the project ships its own onboarding binary instead of leaning on Cloudflare tooling.

**UptimeFlare**, github.com/lyc8503/UptimeFlare. Browser-only flow: click "Use this template", add one Actions secret named `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` (created from the "Edit Cloudflare Workers" token template, with the caveat that D1 Edit permission must be added manually), edit `uptime.config.ts`, and GitHub Actions deploys it; updates are commits. Repo also ships `deploy.tf` using Terraform provider v5. The buttonless "template repo + Actions secret" pattern; it advertises "no local tools required".

**Telegraph-Image**, github.com/cf-pages/Telegraph-Image. Fork, then in the Pages dashboard use "Connect to Git", deploy, then add environment variables (`TG_Bot_Token`, `TG_Chat_ID`, optional KV/R2/AI bindings) under Settings and redeploy. Pure fork-and-dashboard; must be deployed as a Pages project. Representative of the older generation of self-hosted Workers-adjacent apps.

Honest summary of the field: none of the popular projects have a story better than "button for wrangler templates" or "template repo + Actions secret + config file" or "custom npx installer". Nobody in the popular set uses alchemy for consumer-facing deployment.

# 5. Alchemy v2 for reusable, consumer-facing stacks

Sources: https://alchemy.run/ (homepage carries a beta badge), https://alchemy.run/llms.txt (full docs index; no template/catalog section exists), https://alchemy.run/state-store , https://alchemy.run/cli/cloudflare , https://alchemy.run/getting-started , github.com/alchemy-run/alchemy (README marks the project alpha: "Expect breaking changes")

**Status.** alpha/beta, not GA. Providers in the docs: Cloudflare, AWS, GitHub, Neon, PlanetScale, Axiom, Docker.

**Getting started and verbs.** `npx alchemy@latest create --template typescript` scaffolds; `alchemy init` initializes in an existing project. Core verbs: `alchemy plan`, `alchemy deploy`, `alchemy destroy`, `alchemy dev`, `alchemy login` (interactive profiles saved at `~/.alchemy/profiles.json`, browser OAuth or pasted API token, managed with `alchemy login --configure` and `alchemy login --profile <name>`), plus `alchemy tail`, `alchemy logs`, `alchemy nuke`, and `alchemy cloudflare bootstrap / create-token / state logs`. CI uses the `alchemy-run/alchemy@v1` GitHub Action with `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` + `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID`, and gives PR preview stacks named `staging-{number}` with destroy-on-close.

**State stores.** Default is local JSON under `.alchemy/state/<Stack>/<stage>/` (docs tell you to gitignore it; default stage is `dev_$USER`). Remote backends: `Cloudflare.state()` (a one-time-deployed state-store Worker backed by a Durable Object with embedded SQLite; its credentials are generated secrets stored in the account's Secrets Store under `StateStoreSecrets`; bootstrap happens automatically on the first `deploy`/`plan`/`dev`, or manually/idempotently via `alchemy cloudflare bootstrap`, which adopts an existing worker without `--force`; local credentials land in `~/.alchemy/<profile>/cloudflare-state-store.json` and with `CI=true` they are re-resolved from the Secrets Store on every run), and `postgresState({ url })` with an advisory lock per (stack, stage). Custom stores are Effect Layers; KV and R2 are not offered as built-ins.

**Reusable stacks for other people.** There is no catalog, template registry, or share mechanism anywhere in the docs index. The consumption story is structural rather than productized: a stack is plain TypeScript plus an entrypoint file (`alchemy.run.ts`), credentials come from the interactive `alchemy login` profile flow on first deploy, the first deploy itself bootstraps everything (state store, Secrets Store entries), and the `alchemy-run/alchemy@v1` action plus the GitHub provider's "Actions secrets & variables" page (https://alchemy.run/github/actions-config) cover CI. This is what answers the disposable-clone question: with `Cloudflare.state()`, all state lives in the operator's Cloudflare account (state-store Worker + Secrets Store) and profile credentials live in `~/.alchemy/`, so the git clone can be deleted and re-cloned with nothing lost; `alchemy cloudflare bootstrap` is self-healing if the state store itself is damaged.

# Synthesis: what the best achievable UX looks like for a cachet-like alchemy app in mid-2026

Everything below uses only verified mechanisms. The deploy button, C3 remote templates, and Workers Builds auto-provisioning all presuppose a wrangler-config app, so they are closed to an alchemy project today; nothing verified lets a button drive alchemy. The strongest available story is exactly the shape cachet's DEPLOY.md already has, built from these verified parts: a `just bootstrap`-style prompt script (10 vars, 2 secrets, keygen) writing a 0600 env file, then `alchemy deploy`, where the first run interactively logs the operator in via the profile system, auto-bootstraps `Cloudflare.state()` into the operator's own account, provisions R2/KV/worker/cron/custom domain idempotently, and converges on every re-run. That yields the three properties the popular projects each miss half of: Counterscale-grade guided onboarding (via the bootstrap script plus alchemy's login flow), UptimeFlare-grade browser-avoidable credential minimality (one API token; the rest is generated), and a property none of them have: a disposable clone, because state lives remotely and `alchemy cloudflare bootstrap` repairs it. CI follows the alchemy-run/alchemy@v1 action with `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`/`CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` and stage env vars/secrets, with PR preview stages for free. Upgrades are git pull + `alchemy deploy`. The one frontdoor cachet could add without leaving verified ground is optional: a thin wrangler-config "deploy me" shell repo that uses the real Deploy button to provision the Cloudflare side, then hands off to alchemy for everything the button cannot express (custom domain, typed config, secrets prompts) — but the maintainable single-entry answer remains the bootstrap-script + `alchemy deploy` pattern.</result>

All three research tracks are in. The synthesis:

## What the field actually offers (verified against current docs, not memory)

**Cloudflare's first-party distribution is wrangler-shaped and closed to us today.** The Deploy button, C3 remote templates, and Workers Builds all presume a wrangler-config app they can provision bindings from; an alchemy stack declares resources in TypeScript, which none of them read. The popular self-hosted workers projects each ship half a story: R2-Explorer leans on the button (no upgrade path — the clone is a snapshot), UptimeFlare is template-repo-plus-Actions-secret (a fork by another name), and Counterscale ships its own interactive installer (`npx @counterscale/cli install`) — which is the best UX in the field, and it's the one we can beat. Nobody runs alchemy for consumer-facing deployment because alchemy has no consumer-consumption product; but alchemy's *mechanics* are the answer to your custody worry completely for free: with `Cloudflare.state()` (which we already use), the ground truth is a state-store Worker + Secrets Store entries **in the operator's own account**, credentials live in `~/.alchemy/`, first deploy auto-bootstraps it, and `alchemy cloudflare bootstrap` self-heals. The clone is disposable today.

**Custody conventions have converged.** Every serious CLI (`gh`, `wrangler`, `flyctl`, `supabase`, `stripe`) landed on the same shape: interactive setup → `0600` file under a home/XDG path → env var wins as the CI override. Projects that lose clutches gracefully keep config *outside the checkout* (MinIO's `/etc`). And alchemy v2 explicitly takes secrets from the deployer's environment — it defines no custody story, so we define one, once.

**CI without fork has one canonical answer**: a reusable workflow (`workflow_call`). The operator's repo carries ~15 lines, `uses:`-pins our workflow at a tag (Dependabot/Renovate bump it), passes secrets by name, and `environment:` resolves against *their* repo — their reviewer-gated production environment. The precondition is that releases ship a **prebuilt worker bundle** and a **packaged infra program** per tag, because no operator machine should need Rust. The trust caveat is structural: upstream workflow code runs with the operator's secrets, so we document scoped tokens + protected environments + SHA pinning as their side of the deal. (The SLSA generator's scars say our workflows must SHA-pin their own internal `uses:` or SHA-pinning callers break.)

## The design this lands on

**One fact store, outside the clone.** Bootstrap writes `~/.config/cachet/deploy/<stage>.env` at `0600`; `just deploy <stage>` sources in the order: environment > `$CACHET_DEPLOY_CONFIG` > the XDG file > legacy in-clone path (with a deprecation warning). Delete the clone, `git clone`, run again — nothing was ever in it.

**Bootstrap verifies before it writes.** Probe the Cloudflare token against `user/tokens/verify` and refuse an inactive one; format-check the signing key against its printed public half; length-check the OAuth app values and say plainly the secret is proven only at the first real callback. On re-run against an existing deployment, cross-check host/orgs/client-id against the live `/api/public/config` — so "I lost my config" and "re-run bootstrap" are the same runbook, and the only unrecoverable item is the signing key lineage, which already has a documented rotation path. Secrets get no better custody anywhere without forcing a paid vault; this matches what PocketBase/Supabase/Infisical's own docs conclude.

**Vaults are one-line doc entries, never repo code**: `infisical run --env production -- just deploy production`, `op run`, `dotenvx run`, `sops exec-env` — all work because the contract is env vars, full stop. For our org's own Infisical habit (the lynk/maple pattern), that lives in our internal infra repo, not upstream.

**Three operator journeys**:
1. **Their laptop, their daemon**: clone at a release tag → `nix develop` → `just bootstrap` → `just deploy production`. First alchemy run logs them in via profile flow and auto-bootstraps state in their account. Upgrades: `git fetch --tags && git checkout vX.Y.Z && just deploy production`.
2. **Their CI, zero fork**: `.github/workflows/operator-deploy.yml` here, `workflow_call: {cachet-tag, stage}`; their repo calls it pinned; releases publish the prebuilt bundle + infra tarball that the workflow downloads, checksums, and deploys with bun. Your org runs this same path with four environments (`production`, `prod-a`, `prod-b`, `prod-c`) in one infra repo of yours; nothing about that is cachet-specific.
3. **This repo**: deploy.yml stays exactly as testing scaffolding (staging + integration). The integration lane eventually downloads the same release bundle it would ship, so the tested artifact is the shipped artifact.

**Not pursued, with reasons recorded**: the Deploy button / C3 (wrangler-shaped, forks-in-disguise, no upgrade story), Workers Builds (no Rust image, branch-triggered), Pulumi's encrypted-config-in-repo (re-couples custody to the checkout), secret-spec–style resolver abstraction (extra moving parts for a contract `config.ts` already types and validates).

so walk me through how someone who finds this repo woudl setup a full deployment on their own?

A stranger lands on the repo with a Cloudflare account, a zone, and a GitHub org. Here's every step they'd take with today's code, with the two #18/#19 deltas called out where they change the path.

**0. Gather four things (~15 minutes, all one-time).** A Cloudflare API token with the five permission classes DEPLOY.md lists (Workers Scripts:Edit, KV Storage:Edit, R2:Edit, Zone:Read, DNS:Edit) and the account id from the dashboard sidebar. A zone for the domain. The GitHub org slug they serve. A `cache.example.com`-style host name, picked once because it doubles as the signing key's identity and lives in every narinfo signature. Then on GitHub they create an OAuth App in the org — homepage `https://cache.example.com`, callback `https://cache.example.com/_auth/callback`, Device Flow enabled — and keep the client id and secret. Before any cachet command runs, the only tools needed are nix and git.

**1. Clone at a tag, enter the shell.**
```
git clone --branch v0.0.1 https://github.com/nox-systems/cachet.git
cd cachet && nix develop
```
The flake brings every other dependency — bun, wrangler, the worker toolchain — pinned to the repo's exact versions.

**2. `just bootstrap`.** It asks for the host, orgs, admin logins, OAuth client id and secret, and zone answers; generates the signing keypair with `cargo run -p cachet-cli -- keygen`; writes the env file at 0600; prints the public key. *Today* that file is `infra/.env.production` (gitignored, but in the clone); after #18 lands it lives at `~/.config/cachet/deploy/production.env` outside the clone, bootstrap probes the Cloudflare token against `user/tokens/verify` before writing anything, and a re-run cross-checks against the live deployment so bootstrap doubles as the lost-config recovery runbook.

**3. `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=… CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID=… just deploy production`.** One command. It builds the wasm bundle, installs the infra program from its lockfile, and runs the alchemy stack: the first-ever alchemy invocation opens a browser login (or takes the token), then auto-bootstraps the state-store Worker + Secrets Store *in the operator's own account*, then converges R2 bucket, KV namespace, the worker with the two secrets as redacted bindings, the daily 05:00 GC cron, and the custom domain. Rerunning converges again; it never duplicates. The clone can be deleted after this and everything keeps working — state is account-side, bindings are account-side.

**4. Verify (two curls).** `/nix-cache-info` answers; `/api/public/config` answers host, orgs, client id, and the served public key, which must equal what bootstrap printed. If the key doesn't match, stop there.

**5. Wire laptops.** Install the CLI from the release installer (one curl-pipe-sh line in the README), then `cachet login --cache-url https://cache.example.com` (GitHub device flow), `cachet setup` (edits the daemon netrc and `nix.custom.conf`, restarts the daemon), `cachet doctor` (six probes, all `ok`). From then on, nix builds substitute from the deployment with signature verification on.

**6. Wire CI in the served org.** Any repo in the org adds the `uses: nox-systems/cachet/action@v1` step with `id-token: write`. The action installs nix trusting the cache, snapshots the store, and the post step pushes what the build added; the server signs each narinfo after verifying the NAR byte-for-byte. No secrets in the workflow at all.

**7. GC runs by itself.** Armed on the cron from the first deploy, 14-day grace, reports land as objects and serve to admins under `/api/self/gc-runs`. Nothing to configure.

**8. Life after.** Upgrades: checkout the new tag, `just deploy production`. Rollback: checkout the old tag, same command. Key rotation: `cachet keygen --name <host>-2`, swap the var, redeploy, laptops re-run `cachet setup`. Continuous deploys from GitHub Actions instead of a laptop: after #19, the operator's own infra repo holds ~15 lines calling our reusable `operator-deploy.yml@<tag>` with their four secrets; Dependabot opens the upgrade bump as a PR. That's the journey your org would use for its four productions — one infra repo, four environments, no fork of this repo, and Infisical (or anything else) as one env-injecting line in that repo, not in ours.

The total stranger-visible surface: four one-time values, two commands (`bootstrap`, `deploy`), two verification curls, and zero artifacts whose loss would take the deployment down.

`ReadSecret`/`ReadSecretBinding` answer the binding side (a worker CAN bind a Secrets Store secret), and they resolve the confusion: there is no reason we can't keep the values in Cloudflare's store — the thing to be honest about is what that costs, because it's a genuinely different architecture from where the research landed, and it's the better one for the crown jewel that the signing key is.

Your objection is correct on the merits. The XDG file was the *generic* answer (every CLI does it), but generic optimizes for tokens that are scoped and revocable; the signing key is neither — it's the one secret in the system whose theft ships poison until someone notices and rotates. Tying that to a device, in a plaintext-at-rest dotfile that outlives the clone, is exactly the wrong custody. So the design moves to what lynk already does for `ROOT_KEY`:

**The secret never leaves Cloudflare.** Bootstrap mints the keypair and writes the signing key (and the OAuth client secret) into the account Secrets Store directly — from memory, once, no file — and prints only the public key and the re-issue runbook. Routine deploys then carry **zero secret values**: the stack only needs resource names, and the worker binds the store entries by reference. Nothing at rest on the device beyond the Cloudflare API token for that session, which is scoped and dashboard-revocable — a categorically smaller privilege. Your four productions inherit it per-account for free, and rotation becomes a write-new-secret flip instead of a dance over local files. Losing the device loses *nothing*; losing *all* copies just means the documented rotation path, since narinfos are content-addressed and old-key signatures degrade to cache misses.

Three facts price this honestly. First, the Secrets Store is open beta (fine: 100-secret cap, we need three). Second, 🔑: alchemy v2's `SecretsStore.Secret` is a *managed* resource — it demands the value at plan time — so routine-deploy-needs-no-value only holds if the stack binds an existing store entry **by reference**, and whether alchemy's Worker env accepts a raw (store, name) binding descriptor without a managed value is something the package surface doesn't yet answer. Third, the worker runtime change: the binding is `.get()`-at-request-time, not a startup env var, which needs isolate-level memoization against the Clock seam and possibly wasm-bindgen plumbing if workers-rs lacks first-class support — and whether miniflare emulates this binding kind determines if the workerd lane keeps its shape.

That's one small spike, three questions: (1) does the workerd/miniflare binding work locally and remotely, (2) can alchemy bind the secret without holding its value at plan time, (3) what's the memoized-read shape on the signing path. If any answer is no, the fallback is the vault-optional env-injection design (no plaintext at rest for anyone with a wallet, still better than a dotfile), but C is the target. - **The clone-deletion worry gets a two-line answer, not machinery**: the same values belong in the GitHub environment you deploy CI from (or a password manager note), and if everything vanishes the runbook is bootstrap-again + key rotation, which already exists in DEPLOY.md.
- **#19 stands unchanged** — the reusable workflow and per-tag prebuilt bundle are where the "amazing" actually compounds, because that's the difference between an operator maintaining a git surgery habit and merging a Dependabot PR once a release.

Both answers come out of the same two facts: the deployment needs nothing local to *run* (everything lives account-side), and alchemy converges by stage name, so deploys only ever touch the stage you name.

**Scenario 1: deleted the clone, want to upgrade later.** Re-clone at the new tag and re-enter:
```
git clone --branch v0.0.2 https://github.com/nox-systems/cachet.git && cd cachet && nix develop
just bootstrap   # re-derive infra/.env.production
just deploy production
```
The re-run bootstrap is where the recovery smarts live: host, orgs, OAuth client id, and the key prefix all come back from the live deployment's public `/api/public/config`, and the script cross-checks what you answer against it. Alchemy reconnects to the state-store Worker in your account (its credentials survived in `~/.alchemy/`), sees the existing resources, and applies only the new bundle over them — the bucket, the KV namespace, the domain, and every cached object stay exactly where they were.

The one genuinely unrecoverable input is the signing key's secret half, because Cloudflare bindings are write-only. If you stashed `CACHET_SIGNING_KEY` in your password manager or the GitHub environment you deploy CI from (the docs will tell you to do one of these at bootstrap), you paste it back and nothing else changes. If you didn't, the path is the documented rotation: `cachet keygen --name <host>-2`, deploy with the new secret, laptops re-run `cachet setup`. Pre-rotation narinfos then verify as cache misses and rebuild — noisy for a day, never corrupt. The OAuth client secret is the easy half: GitHub's app settings regenerate it on demand.

**Scenario 2: one account, several deployments, updating one.** Stage names are the isolation boundary. Your clone holds one env file per deployment — `infra/.env.production`, `infra/.env.prod-acme` — and every resource alchemy creates is stage-suffixed (`cachet-production` worker/bucket/KV, `cachet-prod-acme` worker/bucket/KV), with per-stage entries in the account state store. So:
```
git checkout v0.0.2
just deploy prod-acme        # converges only cachet-prod-acme-*
```
The production deployment never enters the plan: different resources, different bindings, different state rows, and its own domain and signing key. The only account-shared object is the alchemy state-store Worker itself, which stage deploys never touch. Destroying one (`just destroy prod-acme`) asks confirmation and removes only its stage. Different signing keys also mean clients of one deployment never trust the other — the deployments share an account and nothing else.

So the lifecycle holds up: run forever with no repo, upgrade with a fresh clone plus (at worst) one rotation, and N deployments per account behave like N independent entries in one filing cabinet.
so we probably want a *NAME* associated with the deployments, that `just bootstrap` should ask us about

Yes — and it tightens the whole model rather than adding a concept, because everything except one thing was already waiting for a name:

**What the name binds.** `just bootstrap` asks "deployment name" (grammar: lowercase letters, digits, dashes; starts with a letter; 2–32 chars — the R2 bucket and worker-name rules are the binding constraints). That one answer becomes the env file (`infra/.env.<name>`), the alchemy stage (`just deploy <name>`), and the resource prefix (`cachet-<name>` bucket, KV, worker, state-store rows). `config.ts` is already generic over the stage string and the justfile already takes it as a parameter, so the machinery mostly exists; this makes the name *user-owned* instead of hardcoded to staging/production.

**What the name deliberately does not bind.** The signing key stays `<host>-1:`-named, because host is the protocol identity clients verify — the name is housekeeping. DEPLOY.md should say that once, plainly, so nobody renames a deployment expecting clients to stop verifying.

**One simplification it unlocks.** Today `config.ts` special-cases production (domain defaults to host; other stages must set `CACHET_DEPLOY_DOMAIN`). With named deployments, every deployment has its own host anyway, so the rule flattens: domain defaults to the host *always*, `CACHET_DEPLOY_DOMAIN` is a pure override. That deletes a conditional and a whole error path (the "staging refuses without DOMAIN" refusal in config.ts).

**The one caveat the docs must state**: a name identifies one deployment *per account*. Two operators sharing one Cloudflare account who both name theirs `production` are converging the same stack — not a bug, but it needs saying because "name" invites the intuition that names are free.

Bootstrap's question order becomes: name → host → orgs → admins → OAuth values → keygen → write `infra/.env.<name>` with a header comment carrying the name and date. It folds into #18's reduced scope with the bootstrap-verification work, and `deploy.yml`'s own `staging` naming is unaffected. #!/usr/bin/env bash
# The first-run walkthrough: gather one deployment's identity, verify what
# can be verified, generate the signing keypair, and write infra/.env.<name>
# with everything `just deploy <name>` needs. The GitHub and Cloudflare
# console steps cannot be scripted, so the script prints them as checklists
# at the points where they matter.
#
# The deployment NAME is housekeeping: it names the env file, the alchemy
# stage, and the cachet-<name> resources. The HOST is the protocol identity
# that signs narinfos; renaming the deployment never re-signs anything.
#
# Safe to rerun: it refuses to overwrite an existing file without --force,
# and when the host answers it cross-checks your answers against the live
# deployment's public config, so a rerun against a lost config doubles as
# the recovery path.
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

fail() { echo "cachet: $1" >&2; exit 1; }

preflight() {
  local missing=()
  command -v cargo >/dev/null 2>&1 || missing+=("cargo (run this inside nix develop)")
  command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 || missing+=("jq (run this inside nix develop)")
  command -v curl >/dev/null 2>&1 || missing+=("curl")
  if [ "${#missing[@]}" -gt 0 ]; then
    printf 'cachet: missing: %s\n' "${missing[@]}" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
}

# prompt <question> [default]: answers on stdout, so assign with $(prompt ...).
prompt() {
  local question="$1" default="${2:-}" suffix="" answer
  [ -n "${default}" ] && suffix=" [${default}]"
  printf '%s%s: ' "${question}" "${suffix}" >&2
  read -r answer
  printf '%s' "${answer:-${default}}"
}

preflight

DEPLOYMENT_NAME="$(prompt "Deployment name (lowercase + dashes; one per deployment)" "production")"
[[ ${DEPLOYMENT_NAME} =~ ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{1,31}$ ]] ||
  fail "deployment name must match ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{1,31}\$: resources are named cachet-${DEPLOYMENT_NAME}*"

env_file="infra/.env.${DEPLOYMENT_NAME}"
if [ -e "${env_file}" ] && [ "${1:-}" != "--force" ]; then
  fail "${env_file} already exists; rerun with --force to rebuild it."
fi

CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST="$(prompt "Cache host (the public domain, e.g. cache.example.com)")"
[ -n "${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST}" ] || fail "the host cannot be empty"

# If the token is in the environment, prove it before anything writes:
# a bootstrap that accepts a dead token wastes the rest of the prompts.
if [ -n "${CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN:-}" ]; then
  status="$(curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer ${CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN}" \
    https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/user/tokens/verify | jq -r '.result.status' 2>/dev/null)" ||
    fail "CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN could not reach Cloudflare; check the network and the token."
  [ "${status}" = "active" ] ||
    fail "CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN is ${status}, not active; mint a fresh one (docs/DEPLOY.md lists the scopes)."
else
  echo "cachet: no CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN in the environment; the deploy step needs it (session-scoped, never stored)." >&2
fi

# When the host already answers, its public config is the ground truth:
# on a rerun after losing the file, this is what recovers the non-secret
# values, and on a first run it silently proves nothing and moves on.
served_config="$(curl -fsS --max-time 10 "https://${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST}/api/public/config" 2>/dev/null || true)"

cat >&2 <<CHECKLIST
cachet: bootstrap needs one GitHub OAuth App. In the GitHub org you will
serve, open Settings > Developer settings > OAuth Apps > New OAuth App:

    Application name:               cachet
    Homepage URL:                   https://${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST}
    Authorization callback URL:     https://${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST}/_auth/callback
    Enable Device Flow:             on

Then copy the app Client ID, generate a Client Secret, and have both ready
for the next prompts.
CHECKLIST

CACHET_DEPLOY_ORGS="$(prompt "GitHub org slug(s) to serve, comma-separated")"
CACHET_DEPLOY_ADMINS="$(prompt "Admin GitHub login(s), comma-separated")"
CACHET_DEPLOY_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID="$(prompt "OAuth App client id")"
GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET="$(prompt "OAuth App client secret")"
CACHET_DEPLOY_AUDIENCE="$(prompt "OIDC audience" "cachet")"
CACHET_DEPLOY_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF="$(prompt "Default branch ref" "refs/heads/main")"

for pair in "org slug(s):${CACHET_DEPLOY_ORGS}" "admin login(s):${CACHET_DEPLOY_ADMINS}" \
  "OAuth client id:${CACHET_DEPLOY_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID}" "OAuth client secret:${GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET}"; do
  [ -n "${pair#*:}" ] || fail "the ${pair%%:*} cannot be empty"
done

if [ -n "${served_config}" ]; then
  served_orgs="$(printf '%s' "${served_config}" | jq -r '.orgs | join(",") | ascii_downcase')"
  served_client_id="$(printf '%s' "${served_config}" | jq -r '.oauthClientId')"
  answered_orgs="$(printf '%s' "${CACHET_DEPLOY_ORGS}" | tr -d ' ' | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')"
  if [ "${served_orgs}" != "${answered_orgs}" ] || [ "${served_client_id}" != "${CACHET_DEPLOY_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID}" ]; then
    cat >&2 <<MISMATCH
cachet: the live deployment at ${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST} disagrees with your
answers (orgs: served "${served_orgs}" vs answered "${answered_orgs}";
client id: served "${served_client_id}" vs answered "${CACHET_DEPLOY_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID}").
Continuing writes a divergent deployment; run with --force only if the
config change is the point of this rerun.
MISMATCH
    [ "${1:-}" = "--force" ] || fail "answered values disagree with the live deployment"
  fi
fi

echo "cachet: generating the signing keypair..."
keydir="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "${keydir}"' EXIT
cargo run -q -p cachet-cli -- keygen --name "${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST}-1" --out-dir "${keydir}" >/dev/null
signing_key="$(tr -d '\n' <"${keydir}/cachet-key.secret")"
public_key="$(tr -d '\n' <"${keydir}/cachet-key.public")"
rm -rf "${keydir}"
trap - EXIT

[[ ${signing_key} =~ ^.+:[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{43,44}$ ]] ||
  fail "keygen produced a malformed secret: ${signing_key%%:*}:***"

# A rerun regenerates the pair: if the live deployment serves a DIFFERENT
# public key, writing this file swaps the signing key, and every client's
# trusted-key list must follow (docs/DEPLOY.md's rotation section).
if [ -n "${served_config}" ]; then
  served_key="$(printf '%s' "${served_config}" | jq -r '.publicKey')"
  if [ "${served_key}" != "${public_key}" ]; then
    echo >&2 \
      "cachet: the live deployment serves key ${served_key%%:*}:…, this rerun generated a new pair." \
      "cachet: deploying this file is a KEY ROTATION: clients must rerun cachet setup (
      docs/DEPLOY.md)." >&2
  fi
fi

cat >"${env_file}.tmp" <<ENV
# cachet deployment "${DEPLOYMENT_NAME}" configuration, written by just bootstrap.
# CACHET_SIGNING_KEY never leaves this file and a secret store; keep the
# file at 0600 and never commit it. A second copy in a password manager or
# the CI environment is the recovery answer if this machine dies.
CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST=${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST}
CACHET_DEPLOY_ORGS=${CACHET_DEPLOY_ORGS}
CACHET_DEPLOY_ADMINS=${CACHET_DEPLOY_ADMINS}
CACHET_DEPLOY_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID=${CACHET_DEPLOY_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID}
CACHET_DEPLOY_AUDIENCE=${CACHET_DEPLOY_AUDIENCE}
CACHET_DEPLOY_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF=${CACHET_DEPLOY_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF}
GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET=${GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET}
CACHET_SIGNING_KEY=${signing_key}
# Optional: the future UI's origin for the browser login redirect.
#CACHET_DEPLOY_UI_ORIGIN=https://ui.example.com
ENV
chmod 600 "${env_file}.tmp"
mv "${env_file}.tmp" "${env_file}"

cat <<SUMMARY
cachet: wrote ${env_file} (0600).
cachet: the deployment's public key is:

    ${public_key}

cachet: next steps, in order:

    1. Point the zone running ${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST} at this Cloudflare
       account: the custom domain attaches at deploy time and the zone
       must already exist there.
    2. Keep a second copy of the secrets in ${env_file}: a password
       manager entry, or the CI environment if you deploy from Actions.
       This machine losing the file otherwise means a key rotation
       (docs/DEPLOY.md).
    3. Deploy: CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=... CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID=... just deploy ${DEPLOYMENT_NAME}
       The token needs Workers Scripts:Edit, Workers KV Storage:Edit,
       R2:Edit, Zone:Read, and Zone:DNS:Edit on the zone above.
    4. If GitHub let you set the callback URL only roughly, make sure it
       reads exactly https://${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST}/_auth/callback.
    5. On a laptop: install the cachet binary from the release page, then
       cachet login --cache-url https://${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST}
       cachet setup
       cachet doctor
    6. In CI: uses: nox-systems/cachet/action@v1 with cache-url:
       https://${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST} and permissions id-token: write.

SUMMARY

result.output:
1	# Deploying cachet
2	
3	cachet deploys into your own Cloudflare account. One deployment serves one
4	or more GitHub orgs; stages (`staging`, `production`) are fully separate
5	sets of resources that share nothing. The deploy itself is one command
6	(`just deploy <stage>`); everything below is what surrounds it.
7	
8	## Prerequisites
9	
10	Bring these before the first deploy:
11	
12	1. A Cloudflare account and an API token with Workers Scripts:Edit,
13	   Workers KV Storage:Edit, R2:Edit, Zone:Read, and Zone:DNS:Edit on the
14	   zone that will serve the cache. The account id comes from the
15	   dashboard's right-hand sidebar.
16	2. A zone in that account for the cache's custom domain (for example
17	   `cache.example.com`): production attaches its host name as the
18	   domain, and every other stage names its own through
19	   `CACHET_DEPLOY_DOMAIN`. The host name doubles as the signing key's
20	   name and appears in every narinfo signature, so choose it once.
21	3. A GitHub org whose Actions runners will write to the cache and whose
22	   members will read from it.
23	4. A GitHub OAuth App in that org: homepage `https://<host>`, callback
24	   `https://<host>/_auth/callback`, Device Flow enabled. The callback URL
25	   is fixed by the host, so it can be created before anything deploys.
26	5. The list of GitHub logins that get admin rights (the GC report API).
27	
28	## The first run
29	
30	Run `nix develop`, then `just bootstrap`. It asks for the values above,
31	generates the signing keypair (`cachet keygen`), and writes
32	`infra/.env.production` at mode 0600. That file holds the signing secret
33	and the OAuth client secret; it is gitignored, and it is the canonical
34	local store for them. The printed public key is what laptops will trust.
35	
36	Deploy with the Cloudflare credentials in the environment:
37	
38	```
39	CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=... CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID=... just deploy production
40	```
41	
42	The recipe builds the wasm bundle, installs the infra dependencies from
43	the lockfile, sources `infra/.env.production`, and runs the alchemy
44	stack: R2 bucket, KV namespace, the worker with its bindings, the
45	garbage collector's cron (`0 5 * * *`), and the custom domain. It is
46	idempotent: rerunning converges, it never duplicates.
47	
48	## The configuration contract
49	
50	`just deploy` reads `infra/.env.<stage>` (or exported equivalents).
51	These variables name the deployment:
52	
53	| Variable | Required | Meaning |
54	| --- | --- | --- |
55	| `CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST` | yes | The cache's host name; also the signing key's name prefix. |
56	| `CACHET_DEPLOY_ORGS` | yes | Comma-joined GitHub org slugs; nobody outside them authenticates. |
57	| `CACHET_DEPLOY_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` | yes | The OAuth App's client id. |
58	| `CACHET_DEPLOY_ADMINS` | yes | Comma-joined GitHub logins allowed on `/api/self/*`. |
59	| `CACHET_DEPLOY_AUDIENCE` | no | OIDC audience; default `cachet`. |
60	| `CACHET_DEPLOY_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF` | no | The ref allowed to renew leases; default `refs/heads/main`. |
61	| `CACHET_DEPLOY_DOMAIN` | every non-production stage | Custom domain; production defaults to the host. |
62	| `CACHET_DEPLOY_UI_ORIGIN` | no | Browser login's redirect target; unset answers 204 instead. |
63	| `CACHET_DEPLOY_GC_GRACE_MS` | no | Grace override; staging defaults to 0, elsewhere 14 days. |
64	| `CACHET_SIGNING_KEY` | yes | The `<host>-1:<base64>` secret from bootstrap. |
65	| `GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` | yes | The OAuth App's client secret. |
66	
67	## Staging
68	
69	`just deploy staging` deploys the same stack as `cachet-staging-*` with
70	the GC grace window zeroed, so a seeded object is sweepable on the very
71	next collector tick. Set `CACHET_DEPLOY_DOMAIN` to a staging hostname in
72	your zone (for example `cache-staging.example.com`): the deploy refuses
73	without it, and the integration lane that follows staging deploys needs
74	to know where to point. Use staging to rehearse changes:
75	deploy staging, exercise it, then `just deploy production`. Tear a stage
76	down with `just destroy <stage>`; alchemy asks before deleting.
77	
78	## CI deploys
79	
80	The `deploy` workflow runs staging automatically after a green `ci` on
81	main. Production is manual: Actions > deploy > Run workflow, choosing
82	`production`, and the run waits for the `production` environment's
83	reviewer approval. Configure the two GitHub environments with the same
84	variables the local file carries: `CACHET_DEPLOY_*` as environment
85	variables, `CACHET_SIGNING_KEY`, `GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET`,
86	`CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`, and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` as environment
87	secrets.
88	
89	## Verifying a deployment
90	
91	`curl https://<host>/api/public/config` answers the orgs, the host, the
92	OAuth client id, and the public key; the key must match what bootstrap
93	printed. Then on a laptop: install the CLI with the one-line installer
94	in the README, run `cachet login --cache-url https://<host>`,
95	`cachet setup`, and `cachet doctor`; every probe should print `ok`. The
96	collector fires on the cron, and its runs appear under
97	`/api/self/gc-runs` for an admin.
98	
99	## Rollback
100	
101	Redeploy the previous commit: `git checkout <previous> && just deploy
102	<stage>` converges the stack to that state. The collector's grace window
103	protects cache content through it; leases and reports persist in the
104	bucket, which is stage-scoped, so a rollback never strands state.
105	
106	## Key rotation
107	
108	Rotate the signing key by running `cachet keygen --name <host>-2` (the
109	suffix increments), replacing `CACHET_SIGNING_KEY` in the env file and in
110	the CI secrets, and redeploying. Deployments with clients configured
111	before the rotation must add the new public key: `cachet setup`
112	refreshes the trusted key list from the deployment's public config on
113	re-run.
