content.text: 0009's fixed-pair wording stays as the historical record; 0011 supersedes its grammar point explicitly:

input.content:
# ADR 0011: Deployments are named, and the name is housekeeping

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-08-21
- **Context doc:** [../DEPLOY.md](../DEPLOY.md); supersedes the stage
  grammar of [ADR 0009](0009-alchemy-deployments.md) (its isolation and
  idempotence decisions stand)

## Context

cachet is self-hosted: every operator runs their own deployments, and an
operator may run several in one account (a staging rehearsal, multiple
production caches for different orgs). ADR 0009 framed stages as the
fixed pair `staging`/`production` and special-cased production:
only it defaulted its domain to the host, every other stage refused
without `CACHET_DEPLOY_DOMAIN`, and GC grace defaulted by stage name.
When deployments became a user-facing concept, the fixed pair could not
express "four production deployments in this account", and the
name-keyed special cases pushed deploy behavior into string comparisons.

## Decision

1. A deployment has an operator-chosen name matching
   `^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{1,31}$`, asked for first at `just bootstrap`. The
   name drives the env file (`infra/.env.<name>`), the alchemy stage,
   and the resource prefix (`cachet-<name>` bucket, KV namespace,
   worker). `infra/src/config.ts` enforces the grammar on every deploy,
   so hand-written env files obey it too.
2. The name is housekeeping. The protocol identity stays the host: the
   signing key is `<host>-1`, narinfo signatures name hosts, and
   renaming a deployment never re-signs anything.
3. The custom domain defaults to the host for every deployment;
   `CACHET_DEPLOY_DOMAIN` is a pure override. The production-only
   default and the no-domain refusal are deleted.
4. GC grace defaults to the worker's fourteen days for every deployment;
   throwaway deployments opt into zero explicitly through
   `CACHET_DEPLOY_GC_GRACE_MS`. This repository's own staging pins the
   zero in its deploy workflow, where the reason is readable.
5. One name converges one stack per account: two operators sharing an
   account who both deploy `production` run one shared stack. DEPLOY.md
   carries the caveat.

## Consequences

`just deploy <name>` and `just destroy <name>` need no other changes:
recipes were already parameterized, and bootstrap now owns naming.
Account-side state (ADR 0009's decision) is keyed by stage, so each
name keeps its own state rows and upgrades or destroys one deployment
without touching another. Bootstrap's rerun path doubles as recovery:
the non-secret values regenerate from the live deployment's public
config, and only the two secrets need a second copy kept (password
manager or the CI environment), with rotation as the floor.

## Alternatives considered

Keep the fixed `staging`/`production` pair and let extra deployments be
forks: multiplies review surface for a naming problem; rejected. Make
the deployment name part of the signing identity (`<name>-<host>-1`):
renaming a deployment would rotate client trust for zero protocol
benefit, since signatures answer "which cache signed this", not "which
stack"; rejected. Require `CACHET_DEPLOY_DOMAIN` on every non-production
name (the old rule, generalized): one more first-deploy failure mode
that the host already answers; rejected.

# The operator-facing deploy surface (docs/DEPLOY.md's CI section): an
# operator's own repository calls this workflow pinned to a cachet release
# tag, one GitHub environment per deployment carrying that deployment's
# values. The environment name equals the deployment name, and the
# environment's protection rules (reviewers, branches) apply here exactly
# as if the job lived in the operator's repo — the deployment gate is
# theirs. Secrets arrive explicitly by name; vars resolve inside the
# environment, never at repository level.
name: operator-deploy

on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      cachet-tag:
        description: The cachet release tag to deploy (for example v1.2.3)
        required: true
        type: string
      stage:
        description: The deployment name; also the caller environment's name
        required: true
        type: string
    secrets:
      CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN:
        required: true
      CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID:
        required: true
      CACHET_SIGNING_KEY:
        required: true
      GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET:
        required: true

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  deploy:
    environment: ${{ inputs.stage }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    concurrency:
      # why: one deploy per deployment at a time, and never cancel in
      # flight; a half-updated deployment is worse than a queued one.
      group: cachet-deploy-${{ inputs.stage }}
      cancel-in-progress: false
    env:
      CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN }}
      CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID: ${{ secrets.CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID }}
      CACHET_SIGNING_KEY: ${{ secrets.CACHET_SIGNING_KEY }}
      GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET }}
      CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST: ${{ vars.CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST }}
      CACHET_DEPLOY_ORGS: ${{ vars.CACHET_DEPLOY_ORGS }}
      CACHET_DEPLOY_ADMINS: ${{ vars.CACHET_DEPLOY_ADMINS }}
      CACHET_DEPLOY_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID: ${{ vars.CACHET_DEPLOY_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID }}
      CACHET_DEPLOY_AUDIENCE: ${{ vars.CACHET_DEPLOY_AUDIENCE }}
      CACHET_DEPLOY_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF: ${{ vars.CACHET_DEPLOY_DEFAULT_BRANCH_REF }}
      CACHET_DEPLOY_DOMAIN: ${{ vars.CACHET_DEPLOY_DOMAIN }}
      CACHET_DEPLOY_UI_ORIGIN: ${{ vars.CACHET_DEPLOY_UI_ORIGIN }}
      CACHET_DEPLOY_GC_GRACE_MS: ${{ vars.CACHET_DEPLOY_GC_GRACE_MS }}
    steps:
      - uses: oven-sh/setup-bun@0c5077e51419868618aeaa5fe8019c62421857d6 # v2.2.0
      - name: Fetch and verify the tagged deploy package
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          base="https://github.com/nox-systems/cachet/releases/download/${{ inputs.cachet-tag }}"
          curl -fsSL "${base}/cachet-deploy-${{ inputs.cachet-tag }}.tar.gz" -o cachet-deploy.tar.gz
          curl -fsSL "${base}/cachet-deploy-${{ inputs.cachet-tag }}.tar.gz.sha256" -o cachet-deploy.tar.gz.sha256
          sha256sum -c cachet-deploy.tar.gz.sha256
          tar -xzf cachet-deploy.tar.gz
      - name: Install the infra program from its lockfile
        working-directory: cachet-deploy/infra
        run: bun install --frozen-lockfile
      - name: Deploy
        working-directory: cachet-deploy/infra
        run: bun run deploy --stage "${{ inputs.stage }}"

# Ships the operator deploy package: one tarball per release carrying the
# alchemy program plus the worker bundle built by the flake's pinned
# toolchain, so a deploying operator never builds wasm themselves. Runs
# beside cargo-dist's release.yml (which owns the CLI artifacts); this
# workflow only adds assets to the release it names.
name: release-assets

on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      tag:
        description: The existing release tag to (re)upload the package for
        required: true
        type: string

permissions:
  contents: write

jobs:
  package:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: DeterminateSystems/determinate-nix-action@61cbfe2efc2d4e7a8a6d56967c3c1058e846c858 # v3.21.9
      - name: Build the worker bundle with the pinned toolchain
        run: nix develop --command just wasm
      - name: Package the deploy tarball and checksums
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          tag="${{ github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && inputs.tag || github.ref_name }}"
          pkg="dist/cachet-deploy"
          mkdir -p "${pkg}/crates/cachet-worker"
          cp infra/alchemy.run.ts infra/package.json infra/bun.lock "${pkg}/"
          cp -r infra/src "${pkg}/src"
          cp -r crates/cachet-worker/build "${pkg}/crates/cachet-worker/build"
          asset="cachet-deploy-${tag}.tar.gz"
          (cd dist && tar -czf "${asset}" cachet-deploy)
          (cd dist && sha256sum "${asset}" >"${asset}.sha256")
          echo "ASSET=dist/${asset}" >>"${GITHUB_ENV}"
      - name: Wait for the release and upload
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          tag="${{ github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && inputs.tag || github.ref_name }}"
          for _ in $(seq 1 60); do
            gh release view "${tag}" >/dev/null 2>&1 && break
            sleep 10
          done
          gh release view "${tag}" >/dev/null
          asset="$(basename "${ASSET}")"
          gh release upload "${tag}" "${ASSET}" "dist/${asset}.sha256" --clobber

input.new_string:
## This repository's own deploys

The `deploy` workflow in this repository runs staging automatically
after a green `ci` on main, with the grace window pinned to zero in the
workflow itself so the integration lane can sweep what it seeds.
Production is manual: Actions > deploy > Run workflow, choosing
`production`, and the run waits for the `production` environment's
reviewer approval. Each deployment's GitHub environment carries the same
values the local file carries: the `CACHET_DEPLOY_*` set as environment
variables, and `CACHET_SIGNING_KEY`, `GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET`,
`CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`, and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` as environment
secrets.

## Deploying from your own GitHub Actions

A repository you own can deploy cachet at a release tag without forking
this one: the reusable workflow in
`.github/workflows/operator-deploy.yml` runs a release's deploy package
with your environment's values. One caller workflow plus one GitHub
environment per deployment is the whole setup:

1. Create the deployment first with `just bootstrap` + a manual
   `just deploy <name>` (keys and the OAuth App exist only after it).
   Then create a GitHub environment named exactly the deployment's
   name, carrying the same values the local file carries: the
   `CACHET_DEPLOY_*` set as environment variables, `CACHET_SIGNING_KEY`,
   `GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET`, `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`, and
   `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` as environment secrets. Add required
   reviewers if deploys must wait for approval.
2. Add one caller workflow to a repository you control:

```yaml
name: deploy-cachet
on:
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions: {}

jobs:
  deploy:
    permissions:
      contents: read
    uses: nox-systems/cachet/.github/workflows/operator-deploy.yml@v1.2.3
    with:
      cachet-tag: v1.2.3
      stage: production
    secrets:
      CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN }}
      CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID: ${{ secrets.CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID }}
      CACHET_SIGNING_KEY: ${{ secrets.CACHET_SIGNING_KEY }}
      GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET }}
```

The called workflow downloads the release's deploy package (the alchemy
program plus the worker bundle built from that tag by the pinned
toolchain), verifies its checksum, and runs `bun run deploy --stage
<name>`; the package ships with every release from v0.0.1 on. Upgrading
is a one-line bump of `cachet-tag` and the `uses:` ref, and Dependabot
and Renovate both propose that bump automatically. Pin the `uses:` ref
to a full tag or commit SHA, as with any action.

One honest trust note: a reusable workflow runs upstream-authored code
with your secrets in its environment. The checkpoints are yours: pin the
ref, scope the Cloudflare token to exactly what the deploy needs (the
permission list under Prerequisites), and let the environment's required
reviewers gate production.

content.text: One race-proofing fix before I report: the wait-for-release loop caps at 10 minutes, but cargo-dist's four-target release build can run longer than that on a cold cache — the upload would fail spuriously on the very first tag. Bumping the patience:

input.new_string:
# why: cargo-dist publishes the release only after every CLI
          # target builds, which cold-cache can pass fifteen minutes.
          for _ in $(seq 1 120); do
            gh release view "${tag}" >/dev/null 2>&1 && break
            sleep 10

**Yes — the deployment name should be the bare word.** You answered `staging`, and that's right; it stays verbatim in everything you own: the env file (`infra/.env.staging`), the alchemy stage, the GitHub environment, and — after this fix — the OAuth App's display name. In the dashboard: **My Profile → API Tokens → Create Token → Create Custom Token**, with two resource groups:

- Workers Scripts: **Edit**
- Workers KV Storage: **Edit**

content.text:
Two findings, one of them a real bootstrap defect your rerun just exposed.

**DNS is fine**: `nox.so` is delegated to Cloudflare and `@1.1.1.1` already answers `cachet.staging.nox.so` with Cloudflare proxy IPs. The local "could not resolve" was resolver cache from before the record existed; it clears itself.

**The keys disagree — and that's a bug in my script, not your run.** Your first bootstrap generated key `w9IM…`, the deploy bound *that* into the worker, and then the rerun regenerated a **fresh** pair (`j/xM…`) and overwrote the file. A bootstrap rerun must never silently mint a new identity for an existing deployment. Fixing it now — rerun against the same host carries the existing key forward instead of rotating it:

input.old_string:
echo "cachet: generating the signing keypair..."
keydir="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "${keydir}"' EXIT
cargo run -q -p cachet-cli -- keygen --name "${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST}-1" --out-dir "${keydir}" >/dev/null
signing_key="$(tr -d '\n' <"${keydir}/cachet-key.secret")"
public_key="$(tr -d '\n' <"${keydir}/cachet-key.public")"
rm -rf "${keydir}"
trap - EXIT
input.new_string:
# The signing key is deployment identity, never a byproduct of reruns:
# an existing env file for the SAME host keeps its key (the public half
# derives from the secret's last 32 bytes, no keygen needed), and only a
# missing key or a changed host mints a new pair.
prior_key="" prior_host=""
if [ -e "${env_file}" ]; then
  prior_key="$(sed -n 's/^CACHET_SIGNING_KEY=//p' "${env_file}" | tr -d '[:space:]')"
  prior_host="$(sed -n 's/^CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST=//p' "${env_file}" | tr -d '[:space:]')"
fi

if [ -n "${prior_key}" ] && [ "${prior_host}" = "${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST}" ]; then
  signing_key="${prior_key}"
  public_body="$(printf '%s' "${prior_key#*:}" | base64 -d | tail -c 32 | base64 | tr -d '\n')"
  public_key="${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST}-1:${public_body}"
  echo "cachet: keeping the existing signing key (rerun of an existing deployment; rotate deliberately with cachet keygen instead)." >&2
else
  echo "cachet: generating the signing keypair..."
  keydir="$(mktemp -d)"
  trap 'rm -rf "${keydir}"' EXIT
  cargo run -q -p cachet-cli -- keygen --name "${CACHET_DEPLOY_HOST}-1" --out-dir "${keydir}" >/dev/null
  signing_key="$(tr -d '\n' <"${keydir}/cachet-key.secret")"
  public_key="$(tr -d '\n' <"${keydir}/cachet-key.public")"
  rm -rf "${keydir}"
  trap - EXIT
fi

wait why arent the env varibale names prefixed with CACHET_*

Because those two names are not ours to choose — they're Cloudflare's own contract. `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` are what wrangler, alchemy's auth layer, C3, and every Cloudflare tutorial read natively. Prefixing them `CACHET_` would rename the variable for exactly zero parties: the tools that consume them wouldn't read the new name, and we'd have to bridge the standard names back in anyway (maple's codebase literally carries that bridge from an older org-specific name to the standard one).

So the actual rule the repo follows, now that it's had a chance to be said plainly: **cachet names every contract cachet owns** (`CACHET_DEPLOY_*`, `CACHET_SIGNING_KEY`, `CACHET_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET`, `CACHET_INTEGRATION_*`) and **leaves outside ecosystems' names to the outside** — Cloudflare's pair, the Actions runner's `GITHUB_REF`/`ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_*`, XDG's paths. Today's `GITHUB_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET` rename was the same rule in reverse: we left a name inside someone else's reserved prefix and got rejected; you don't squat on `GITHUB_*`, and you don't repaint `CLOUDFLARE_*`.

1. `ci` runs the full matrix on the pushed SHA.
2. When it greens, `deploy` fires automatically and its `staging` job **checks out that exact commit**, rebuilds the wasm bundle from it, and runs `just deploy cachet-staging` — alchemy converges the staging worker to the new bundle, using the environment's values for everything that isn't code.
3. The `integration` job then exercises **that fresh deployment**: real OIDC, push of a run-tagged path through the built-from-source CLI, delete, `nix copy --from` with nix verifying the signature.

So every green main is: new code ships to staging → e2e proves the new code. You never touch the environment again unless a *value* changes (rotate a key, add an org) — version-to-version, it's inert drawer contents, while the moving part is whatever you merged.

The same architecture is what an operator gets through `operator-deploy.yml`, except their code comes from the tag's prebuilt package instead of a per-push rebuild.

From your local file, over a sealed channel, while you watched. When you said "you do it," I read each value out of `infra/.env.cachet-staging` (the 0600 file bootstrap had written) and piped it into GitHub's CLI without ever printing it:

```

`gh secret set` reads stdin, encrypts the value client-side against the environment's libsodium public key, and uploads only the ciphertext — so the plaintext path for both secrets was: keygen/OAuth console → your 0600 file → sealed write into GitHub's store. The terminal transcript shows only `secret <NAME>: set`, which is why nothing sensitive ever appeared in this conversation. Both values are write-only from here on; `gh secret list --env cachet-staging` will show names and timestamps, never bodies.

That's also the general custody rule for this rig: the file on your laptop and the GitHub environment are the two readable homes, and anything that needs the values (your deploys, CI's deploys) reads through one of them — the worker never gets them any other way.

    [ -n "$ci_id" ] && echo "ci run for 5738c24: $ci_id"
  else
    ci_s=$(gh run view "$ci_id" --json status,conclusion --jq '"\(.status) \(.conclusion)"' 2>/dev/null || true)
    ci_con=$(echo "$ci_s" | awk '{print $2}')
    if [ "$ci_con" = "success" ]; then
      echo "ci 5738c24 GREEN; deploy chain armed"
      if [ -z "$deploy_id" ]; then
        deploy_id=$(gh run list --repo nox-systems/cachet --branch main --workflow deploy --limit 3 --json databaseId,headSha --jq '.[] | select(.headSha | startswith("5738c24")) | .databaseId' | head -1)
        [ -n "$deploy_id" ] && echo "deploy run: $deploy_id"
      fi
    elif [ "$ci_con" = "failure" ] || [ "$ci_con" = "cancelled" ]; then
      echo "ci 5738c24 ${ci_con} — the chain stalls here"; break
    fi
  fi
  if [ -n "$deploy_id" ]; then
    st=$(gh run view "$deploy_id" --json status,conclusion,jobs --jq '[.status, .conclusion, ([.jobs[] | "\(.name):\(.conclusion // .status)"] | join(","))] | join(" ")' 2>/dev/null || true)
    dcon=$(echo "$st" | awk '{print $2}')
    case "$dcon" in
      success|failure|cancelled) echo "deploy chain TERMINAL: $st"; break;;
    esac
  fi
  sleep 45
done

There's a lot of these `building` lines in CI. Does that mean once cachet is enabled on these CI runs they'll automatically get cached?

Those lines are each fresh CI runner re-fetching the pinned toolchain (the `.tar.xz` fixed-output fetches from rust's dist CDN) and then rebuilding anything not already in *its own* empty store — per-job, every push, because GitHub runners start cold. Nothing is shared between jobs today.

The answer to your question is "yes, but with a wiring step named," and the nuance matters:

**What cachet does for this**: a nix binary cache substitutes store paths instead of building them. The moment our ci jobs subscribe to a cachet deployment (substituter + its public key in the nix config — exactly what our own action does for consumer repos) AND something pushes what a run built, every later run substitutes instead of re-downloading rust-std or recompiling the workspace. First run after wiring warms it; every run after is the payoff.

**The honest "automatically" asterisks**:
- It starts working only once the CI is wired: the action that installs nix-trusting-the-cache is itself a released artifact — it exists the day you tag `v0.0.1`. That's the dogfooding circle closing: the repo's own ci becomes cachet's best first customer, pointing at a deployment whose org (`nox-systems`) and OIDC it already passes.
- The current staging deployment publishes GC with grace **zero** for the lane's sake — but cache content survives because **leases** pin it, not grace: pushes keyed to `main` renew their closure's lease every green run, so toolchain + workspace paths stay live while only the integration lane's throwaway payloads ever get swept. That design point is doing real work here.
- One factual note on these specific lines: `.tar.xz` "building" steps are fixed-output derivations — once pushed, they substitute from cachet the same as any other store path; the per-run re-download from rust-lang.org just stops happening.

Sequence-wise it lands as: tag → wire `ci.yml` to trust the deployment + add the action step → one warming run → every future run's toolchain and dependency builds collapse into substitutions. Want that wired as the first post-tag commit?

content.text:
Full incident story, sealed:

**What the chain taught us today**: ci `55ef7d4` green → the staging converge **succeeded pulling every value from secrets** (your swap's proof) → integration failed at its OIDC probe with 503 — the first thing the lane ever caught in the wild, on its first run, exactly as designed.

**Root cause**: `fetch_jwks` treated `CACHET_JWKS_URL` as mandatory; the whole workerd matrix injects that var (it's how stubs substitute GitHub), so "var absent" never existed in testing — until production, where alchemy correctly sets nothing. The class audit found three of them: the JWKS URL plus `CACHET_GITHUB_API_URL` and `CACHET_GITHUB_WEB_URL` — verdicts and browser login were broken the same way.

**The fix** (`9116141`): the three defaults are now cachet-core constants (`api.github.com`, `github.com`, the OIDC issuer's JWKS path) served through one pure `override_or` resolver whose unit tests pin absent/blank/set semantics; the worker's three call sites read override-or-default. `gc.rs` had this pattern right all along; one clippy drive-by removed a now-always-Ok `Result` return. The coverage story says itself out loud: unit tests own override semantics, workerd owns stub behavior, integration owns the live default — the middle layer genuinely cannot cover "var absent" hermetically, which is the integration lane's charter.

**Now**: the chain re-runs against the fixed worker. ci → staging converge → integration. If integration gets past the OIDC probe, the remainder of the lane (push, delete, signature-verified substitute) is new territory that local lanes already cover — but live is live, and I'll read whatever the wire says.
